considering the inherent variability of these assays.
: To minimize unnecessary sacrifice of animals, we aimed to use the minimal number of
mice required for our study. To assess whether our dataset deviated significantly from
normality, we performed a normality test.
Most behavioral datasets followed a normal distribution (see below). However, the dataset
from exercised WT mice expressing lentivirus S1eKO (LV-hCas9:T2A:Puro-U6>gRNA-
U6>gRNA) did not pass the normality test.
Therefore, we used a non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis test to analyze whether the reduced
expression of muscle-derived Serpina1e affects exercise-induced memory enhancement
(Fig. 4l in the revised manuscript).
Despite the limited sample size in the behavioral assays, we observed significant changes
in memory performance following muscle Serpina1e manipulation.
Additionally, we have revised and expanded the details of statistical tests in the Methods
section of the revised manuscript.
8. The assessment of cognitive function is done with novel object recognition and with
fear conditioning. However, there are other assays, such as the Morris water maze,
listed in the methods but no data with these assays is reported in the figures for Serpina
1e (only a supplementary figure reports positive effects of exercise with this assay).
The authors should perform this gold-standard assay for at least one of their models of
Serpina 1e modulation.
: We acknowledge that the Morris water maze is a well-established test for assessing
spatial learning and memory. However, other behavioral tests, such as contextual fear
conditioning (CFC) and novel object recognition (NOR), are also widely recognized
methods for evaluating hippocampus-dependent cognitive functions.
We also observed that skeletal muscle-specific reduction of Serpina1e expression prevents
the exercise-induced improvement in memory retrieval in both the NOR and CFC tests (Fig.
4k, l in the revised manuscript). Furthermore, the same manipulation abolishes the
exercise-induced increase in the number of NeuN/BrdU double-positive cells (Fig. 6g, h in
the revised manuscript).
Therefore, these findings not only highlight the beneficial and essential roles of muscle-
derived Serpina1e in hippocampal memory through the promotion of neurogenesis but also
support the notion that NOR and CFC tests are equally effective as the Morris water maze
in evaluating exercise-modulated hippocampal cognitive functions.
9. In Fig. 5a, the authors report that V5-tagged Serpina 1e that is retro-orbitally injected
can reach the CSF and the hippocampus. However, the authors should also monitor the
total levels of Serpina 1e (injected + endogenous) to determine whether the injection of
Serpina 1e indeed increases the total levels of Serpina 1e in the CSF and hippocampus.
For these studies, they can utilize the anti-Serpina 1 antibody used in Fig. 4f.
: As the reviewer suggested, we attempted to detect changes in total Serpina1e protein
levels (injected + endogenous) in the hippocampus following administration of
recombinant Serpina1e-V5 protein by using anti-Serpina1 antibody targeting.
Consistent with our findings in original study, we detected a significant increase in total
plasma Serpina1 level from mice administered with Serpina1e-V5 (Supplementary Fig.
16d, e in the revised manuscript). Further analysis with CSF collected from mice with
Serpina1e-V5 administration revealed that total Serpina1 is slightly increased
(Supplementary Fig. 16f in the revised manuscript), although western blot analysis with
CSF was not fully replicated due to the limited number of available mice.
We next attempted to detect total Serpina1 level in hippocampal extract from mice with
Serpina1e-V5 administration. Despite some non-specific signals, our western blot results
showed a weak but significant anti-Serpina1 signal in hippocampal extracts from mice
administered with Serpina1e-V5. The detected band matched the expected size of
the Serpina1e-V5 protein and the detected Serpina1 band in plasma (Supplementary Fig.
16d, g-i in the revised manuscript).
Importantly, this corresponding signal was absent in hippocampal extracts from control
(PBS-injected) mice, suggesting that endogenous Serpina1 protein levels in the
hippocampus are negligible or too low to be detected by western blot. This finding aligns
with publicly available data, such as the Human Protein Atlas
(https://www.proteinatlas.org/ENSG00000197249-SERPINA1), which reports that both
mRNA and protein levels of endogenous SERPINA1 are very low in the hippocampus
compared to other tissues.
On the same line, they should also monitor whether exercise modulates the CSF and
hippocampal levels of Serpina 1e.
: As suggested by the reviewer, we attempted several times to detect changes in
total Serpina1 protein levels by performing western blot analysis on hippocampal extracts
using a pan-Serpina1 antibody. However, we were unable to detect any significant signal
corresponding to the expected size of Serpina1 proteins in all groups of mice (please see
the image below).
We suspect that this result is due to the concentration of hippocampus-transmitted
Serpina1(e) being too low to be detected using conventional antibody-based methods such
as western blot. Despite this negative finding, we have already demonstrated that
systemically administered recombinant Serpina1e protein can be detected in the
hippocampus (Fig. 5c,d; Supplementary Fig. 16 in the revised manuscript). This
suggests that Serpina1e is indeed capable of crossing from the bloodstream into the
hippocampus.
10. In Figure 6, the authors report that Serpina 1e injection increases cell proliferation
in the hippocampus and BDNF levels (by 10%). Are there corresponding changes in
BDNF protein levels? This looks overall as a minor effect.
: The BDNF levels shown in Fig. 6c of the original manuscript were measured using an
ELISA assay and directly correspond to BDNF protein levels in the hippocampus. To avoid
any confusion, we will clearly indicate this in the revised manuscript (line 269).
BDNF protein exists at relatively low concentrations, however, even subtle changes in its
levels are known to effectively influence downstream signaling via its high-affinity receptor,
TrkB (Kd ~ 10⁻¹¹ M; Rodrigues-Tebar et al., 1990, Neuron, 4:487-92). Previous studies
have reported that BDNF protein is detectable at 108–256 ng/g of tissue in the
hippocampus, frontal cortex, and neostriatum of the rodent brain (Radka et al., 1996, Brain
Research, 709:122-301). Furthermore, treating cultured hippocampal neurons with as little
as 20 ng/ml of recombinant BDNF is sufficient to elicit BDNF-TrkB-dependent neurite
growth (Righi et al., 2000, J. Neurosci., 20:3165-3174). Additionally, a recent study
demonstrated that even a ~10% change in BDNF levels can alter dendritic growth and
rescue memory impairment induced by hypoxic stress (Li et al., 2025, Sci. Rep., 15:1135).
On the other hand, BDNF secretion and clearance have been reported to occur on the
scale of seconds to minutes (Bergami et al., 2008, JCB, 183:213-221; Han et al., 2021, Sci.
Rep., 11:21203; Park and Poo, 2013, Nat. Rev. Neurosci., 14:7-23), indicating the rapid
and transient kinetics of BDNF concentration in the brain. These unique properties of BDNF
may lead to an underestimation of the extent to which Serpina1 upregulates BDNF when
measured using hippocampal extracts and antibody-based detection methods such as
ELISA.
11) It is unclear mechanistically how Serpina 1e would modulate BDNF levels, cell
proliferation, and neurite outgrowth. What is the receptor mediating the action of
Serpina 1e?
: The receptor for Serpina1e in the brain is totally unknown and remains to be identified. In
peripheral tissues, such as adipocytes, mouse Serpina1 proteins have been reported to
interact with Ephrin type-B receptor 2 (EphB2). This interaction could elicit cell proliferation
and lead to UCP1-induced improvements in thermogenesis and glucose metabolism
(Okagawa et al., 2024, Nature Communications, 15:9585). However, whether EphB2 is
associated with the beneficial effects of Serpina1e on growth signaling has not yet been
examined. Further investigation is required to elucidate the molecular mechanisms
underlying Serpina1e-induced neuronal growth signaling and cognitive enhancement.
We have included additional discussion about the expected downstream signaling of
Serpina1e in the brain in Discussion of the revised manuscript (line 338 ~ 360).
12) The statistical analysis does not seem to be always appropriate. For example,
the data in Fig. 4b was analyzed by Student’s t-test but there are 2 variables (before
and retrieval) for 2 groups (saline and serpina) and therefore should be analyzed by
2-way ANOVA. This applies also to other graphs such as Fig. 4e and Fig. 5g.
: As the reviewer suggested, a two-way ANOVA with Sidak’s post hoc test was used for
contextual conditioning tests in Fig. 4b, 4e, 4l, and 5g in the revised manuscript. Other
data in Supplementary Fig. 10b, 11b, and 12b in the revised manuscript were tested
with a two-way ANOVA with Sidak’s post hoc test.
The change from one-way ANOVA to two-way ANOVA did not result in any changes in the
conclusion of our findings. We have also included detailed information of the statistical
analysis in the Methods of the revised manuscript.
Additional points:
13) There is no loading control (such as Ponceau) for the western blot in Fig. 1e.
: We added ponceau stained membrane image in Fig. 1e in the revised manuscript.
14) In Fig. 2 the authors report a global increase in myokines in the plasma in
response to exercise. However, how is this data normalized to ensure that this is
indeed the case?
: To guide the normalization strategy for LC-MS experiments, we were hinted from Western
blot analysis results.
During Western blot analysis, equal amounts of the plasma fraction acquired from AcTuR
mice were loaded to estimate the total amount of input plasma proteins and the abundance
of biotinylated proteins in plasma. Because the overall intensities of Ponceau staining were
comparable, we assumed that the total input proteins are comparable across all
experimental groups (Fig. 1e, right, in the revised manuscript). However, the levels of
biotinylated proteins were increased in plasma samples from mice provided with biotin, and
the overall amounts of biotinylated proteins were further elevated when exercise was
introduced (Fig. 1e-f in the revised manuscript).
Based on this result, sample preparation for LC-MS/MS analysis was performed with an
equal amount of plasma from each experimental group/mouse as in the Western blot
analysis had been done, to ensure the consistency of the amounts of total plasma proteins.
All samples were processed in parallel to minimize variability and maintain experimental
rigor. When the biotinylated proteome samples were ready, we consistently used the
identical fraction of samples (50% of each sample) for LC-MS/MS analysis, and the
quantification of biotinylated proteins was performed based on label-free quantification
(LFQ) (Cox et al., 2014, Mol. Cell. Proteomics, 13: 2513-2526). Once we obtained the
quantification result of biotinylated proteins, we did not perform any further post-
normalization of the quantified dataset.
Consistent with the Western blot analysis, LC-MS/MS data demonstrated a reproducible
increase in overall biotinylated protein levels upon biotin supplementation, with a further
enhancement observed following exercise combined with biotin supplementation
(Supplementary Fig. 7c in the revised manuscript, ****p<0.0001, one-way ANOVA with
Dunnett’s post hoc test), as shown in Fig. 1e-f in the revised manuscript.
As these two independent experiments showed consistent results, we confirmed that our
observations accurately reflect the actual phenomenon of increased secretion of
biotinylated myokines from muscle upon exercise.
This additional result and description of protein quantification are now updated in
Supplementary Fig. 7 and Methods in the revised manuscript.
15) It is unclear what is the control in Fig. 5e-g.
: Control mouse was injected with the same volume of PBS instead of Serpina1e-V5.
This information is now included in the legend of Figure 5 and Methods in the revised
manuscript.
16) The discussion of scientific background is a bit limited. The authors should better
discuss studies that have examined communication between the skeletal muscle and
the brain.
: We thank the reviewer for helpful comment to improve our manuscript.
Now the revised manuscript includes the summary of previous studies showing functional
roles and related mechanisms of exercise-induced myokines such as FNDC5/irisin and
CTSB in brain functions in the Discussion of the revised manuscript.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript Kim and colleagues identify Serpina1e as a myokine that is released
by muscle into the plasma following 4 weeks of exercise. The also show that delivery
of Serpina1e into the plasma, muscle or hippocampus can replicate the hippocampus-
associated learning and memory enhancement observed following exercise. Overall,
this is a very interesting study. However, several key points should be addressed before
this manuscript would be suitable for publication in Nature Communications.
Major questions:
1. The title of the paper states that Serpina1e “mediates” the exercise-induced
enhancement of hippocampal memory. Likewise, in the abstract they state that
Serpina1e…..”directly” supports long-term memory formation. I disagree that the data
presented here shows this. The authors show that Serpina1e is released by muscle
a muscle after exercise and that Serpina1e
delivery can enhance cognition. However, whether Serpina1e is responsible/required for the exercise-induced
enhancement in cognition has not been shown. To show this direct relationship, one would for example need to knock out
Serpina1e in the muscle and show that exercise can no longer enhance cognition. These statements should all be toned down throughout the manuscript, including the title.
: We thank the reviewer for the valuable comment.
To support our conclusion that Serpina1e mediates exercise-induced enhancement of
hippocampal memory, we tested whether exercise-induced cognitive improvements are
prevented by the reduced Serpina1e expression in skeletal muscles.
To achieve this, we produced a lentivirus containing hCas9 and two gRNAs targeting
Serpina1e (LV-hCas9:T2A:Puro-U6>gRNA-U6>gRNA; S1eKO). This lentivirus was
injected into the limb muscles of wild-type mice, while the lentivirus expressing EGFP and
mCherry (LV-EGFP:T2A:Puro-EF1a>mCherry) was used as a control. Semi-quantitative
RT-PCR analysis of limb muscles injected with the S1eKO lentivirus confirmed that
Serpina1e transcript levels were significantly reduced (Supplementary Fig. 15a-d; Fig.
4h-j in the revised manuscript).
Next, wild-type mice injected with either the S1eKO or control lentivirus were subjected to
novel object recognition (NOR) and contextual fear conditioning (CFC) tests after four
weeks of wheel-running exercise. Our results showed that S1eKO-injected animals without
exercise exhibited normal basal activity and hippocampal memory, indicating that muscle-
derived Serpina1e in non-exercised animals does not affect overall behavioral or cognitive
functions (Fig. 4k, l; Supplementary Fig. 15e-i in the revised manuscript). However,
S1eKO-injected animals failed to show enhanced memory retrieval in NOR and CFC tests,
indicating that exercise-induced cognitive enhancement requires muscle-derived
Serpina1e (Fig. 4k, l in the revised manuscript). Taken together with the results from the
original manuscript, this additional data supports our conclusion that muscle-derived
Serpina1e mediates exercise-induced cognitive enhancement.
2. The authors state that Serpina1e delivery increases neurogenesis in the hippocampal
dentate gyrus. From the data presented in Figure 6 b one is not able to draw this
conclusion. BrdU was injected for the last 5 days of prior to perfusion and BrdU+ cells
quantified. These BrdU+ cells will be a mixture of proliferating neural precursor cells,
immature neurons that may have already become post-mitotic since the first injection
5 days prior, proliferating microglia etc. To be able to quantify adult neurogenesis it
would be best to inject BrdU at the start of the experiment and quantify BrdU+NeuN+
double-positive cells. Alternatively, on the available sections a proliferation marker
such as Ki67 could be used to quantify the proliferating cells (ideally co-labelled with
other markers such as Tbr2 or Sox2) and the immature newborn neurons could be
quantified using DCX staining.
: As the reviewer suggested, we re-assessed the amount of neurogenesis stimulated by
Serpina1e delivery by measuring BrdU/NeuN-double positive cells in the mouse
hippocampus following Serpina1e administration. Our new immunohistochemistry results
showed an increased number of BrdU/NeuN-double positive cells after Serpina1e
administration, while the number of BrdU+/NeuN- cells was unaffected (Fig. 6c-f in the
revised manuscript). These results indicate that Serpina1e-evoked proliferating cells are
neuronally differentiated.
In our experiment, BrdU injection was started 5 days before brain harvest, as done
previously, to examine the effect of chronic Serpina1e administration on neurogenesis. As
the reviewer pointed out, exercise is effective for both the survival and proliferation of
hippocampal neurons (van Praag, 2008, NeuroMolecular Medicine, 10-128-140). Many
studies have shown that chronic exercise (at least three weeks or longer) is most efficient
for the proliferation and survival of hippocampal neurons, as demonstrated by BrdU labeling
at the start of the exercise training. On the other hand, our results, with BrdU injection
starting 5 days prior to the end of Serpina1e administration, reveal only the effect of
Serpina1e on the proliferation of hippocampal cells, not the survival of newborn neurons.
Whether Serpina1e is also effective in upregulating the survival of newborn neurons
remains unclear. Given the crucial role of BDNF signaling in cell survival and the increased
BDNF level after 4 weeks of Serpina1e administration (Fig. 6b in the revised manuscript),
it is possible that Serpina1e administration may also be beneficial for the survival of
newborn neurons.
Additionally, it is unclear if the BrdU counts presented in Fig 6b are per section or per
DG. There is no information in the methods about which sections were stained with
BrdU (i.e., a 1 in 6 series through the whole brain or alike). It is stated that cells were
counted from 12 sections – how were these sections chosen?
: To count the number of BrdU-positive cells, six series of DG slices (at intervals of 120 µm)
from the dorsal hippocampus of each hemisphere (12 sections per mouse) were selected.
The BrdU(+)/NeuN(+) and BrdU(+)/NeuN(-) cell numbers from the six DG slices in each
hemisphere were averaged to produce the mean cell numbers, which are shown as
individual dots in the bar graph (Fig. 6d-f in the revised manuscript).
This detailed information on image analysis has now been included in the Methods section
of the revised manuscript (line 743~747).
The counts state they are # cells/DG and are around 20-30, which if it is BrdU cells per
DG I would expect this count to be hundreds from a young mouse.
: There was our mistake in Fig. 6b in the original manuscript.
The range of Y-axis should be 0-20, and it is now corrected in Fig. 6d in revised
manuscript. This result is consistent with previous reports that the mean number of BrdU-
positive cells in the hippocampus of adult mice is around 15 cells (Zhang et al, 2016, Mol
Med Rep, 14:2231-2237; Kang et al, 2018, Exp Neurobiol, 27(5):419-436).
3. Changes in dendritic arborization could also be assessed in the same mice in the
newborn neurons by performing Sholl analysis on DCX+ cells in vivo. This would
significantly strengthen the in vitro finding which was performed on embryonic cortical
neurons rather than those from the adult hippocampus.
: Instead of DCX staining, we evaluated dendritic arborization in the hippocampal CA1 and
DG areas by measuring Microtubule-associated protein 2 (MAP2)-positive dendrites, as
MAP2 is known to be highly enriched in the dendritic compartment and strongly associated
with branched neurites (Chamak et al., 1987, J Neurosci, 7(10):3163-3170; Chou et al.,
2024, eLife13:RP103127).
To increase the plasma level of Serpina1e, we overexpressed Serpina1e in skeletal
muscles by delivering an AAV virus expressing Serpina1e-EGFP (AAV9-CMV-
mSerpina1e:T2A:EGFP) into the four limbs of WT mice. Control mice were injected with
AAV9-CMV-EGFP. This intramuscular overexpression of Serpina1e was sufficient to
elevate Serpina1e mRNA expression in skeletal muscles and plasma Serpina1e protein
levels (Fig. 4f-g; Supplementary Fig. 14 in the revised manuscript), as well as
hippocampal memory performance (Fig. 4c-e in the revised manuscript). Given our
findings that plasma Serpina1e can be delivered to the hippocampus by crossing the blood-
CSF and blood-brain barriers (Fig. 5a-d; Supplementary Fig. 16 g-i in the revised
manuscript), this intramuscular overexpression of the Serpina1e gene is expected to
upregulate hippocampal Serpina1e protein levels and serve as a useful model for testing
the in vivo effects of Serpina1e on neurite growth.
Z-stack images of MAP2-positive dendrites (775.19 µm x 775.19 µm x 7 µm) were 2D-
projected with maximum intensity to compare the complexity of CA1 dendrites, represented
by MAP2 intensity, between control and muscle Serpina1e-overexpressed mice. Our
results show that the average MAP2 intensity in the hippocampal CA1 and DG area of
muscle Serpina1e-overexpressed mice is significantly higher than that of control mice
(Supplementary Fig. 18 in the revised manuscript). These results indicate that
Serpina1e promotes neuronal dendritic growth in vivo and is consistent with in vitro finding
of elevated neurite growth following treatment with recombinant Serpina1e protein in
cultured neurons.
4. Why were only male mice used in the study? This should be stated in the abstract
and discussed in the discussion.
: To avoid any unexpected effects of sex-dependent physiological and behavioral
phenotypes, we only used male mice in this study.
As human SERPINA1 gene is reported to be a direct target of estrogen receptor and a
predictor of survival rate in patients with breast cancer (Chan et al., 2016, Oncotarget. 6:
25815-25817), it is possible that Serpina1e-induced effects can be influenced by sex-
specific biological mechanisms. Future studies will need to consider comparative
investigations of Serpina1e-mediated cognitive modulation in both sexes.
As the reviewer suggested, we include the statement of the usage of male mice and the
future need of studies addressing the sex-specific role of Serpina1e in cognitive modulation,
in the Abstract (line 27) and Discussion (line 375~376) in the revised manuscript.
Minor points:
1. In the abstract, it is stated that “the beneficial effects of exercise on cognitive
function appear to be mediated by muscle-derived secretory factors”. While muscle is
certainly an important tissue that exerkines are secreted from, there are many others
i.e. hepatokines, adipokines etc.
: Agreeing with the reviewer’s point. We have revised the abstract as following:
line 19: The exercise-induced enhancement of learning and memory is thought to be
regulated not only by improved cardiometabolic and psychosocial health but also
by body‒brain interactions mediated by metabolites and proteins derived from
peripheral organs. Given the prominent role of skeletal muscle during exercise,
muscle-derived factors are believed to mediate the cognitive enhancements induced
by exercise.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The manuscript titled "Serpina1e mediates the exercise-induced enhancement of hippocampal memory" presents robust and novel findings identifying Serpina1e as a key myokine mediating the cognitive benefits of exercise. The study is methodologically sound, with comprehensive in vivo and in vitro validation, and the conclusions are well supported by the data.
The work is highly significant for the field, offering insights comparable to previous discoveries such as Irisin, and expanding our understanding of muscle-brain communication. The authors satisfactorily addressed reviewer comments, improving the clarity, methodological transparency, and discussion of their findings. The experimental design, data analysis, and reporting meet the expected standards, with sufficient detail provided to ensure reproducibility. In my evaluation, the manuscript is ready for publication without further revisions.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors have made improvements to this interesting manuscript; however, I remain skeptical about several key findings due to significant limitations in both the previous and newly added data.
1) The authors did not conduct the straightforward analysis I requested (previous point 3) to assess whether muscle-contributed Serpina1 is a significant source of the systemic Serpina1 pool, which is primarily expressed in the liver. The authors have access to pan-Serpina1 antibodies and mass spectrometry that could be used for these analyses. At present it remains uncertain whether Serpina 1e secreted by muscle significantly contributes to the circulating pool of Serpina 1e and total Serpina1.
2) The authors now suggest that the muscle pool of Serpina1e plays a key role because they injected lentiviral vectors to knock out Serpina1 in 4 limb muscles, which they claim prevents exercise-induced changes in behavior (discrimination index and freezing). However, these experiments (Fig. 4h-l, as well as others such as those in Fig. 7a-h) are conducted suboptimally, as a control exercise group is not included, leaving it unclear whether the exercise training was performed at optimal levels to induce a response. Additionally, there is no evidence that the lentiviral vectors used are muscle-specific, as they do not appear to carry a muscle-specific promoter and could potentially target Serpina1e in the liver or other tissues. Finally, even if the authors' model is correct and Serpina1e is indeed specifically knocked out in 4 limb muscles, it is still uncertain how this could impair the beneficial effects of exercise on the brain, given that many other muscles, both in the limbs and throughout the body, remain unaffected by the lentiviral vectors (Serpina1e should still increase following exercise in the vast majority of these muscles which are not targeted by the lentiviral vectors and hence promote exercise-induced improvements in behavior).
3) As mentioned in my previous comments, the cognitive assays that are currently utilized in the manuscript (novel object recognition and fear conditioning) are inherently variable. Robust gold-standard assays such as the Morris Water Maze should be performed for at least some of the key experiments.

our manuscript, “Serpina1e mediates the exercise-induced enhancement of
hippocampal memory” (NCOMMS-24-60831-A) by Kim et al.” is now suitable for
publication in Nature Communications.
However, Reviewer #3 still raised several concerns regarding our findings and requested
additional evidence to support our conclusion. Specifically, Reviewer #3 asked us to provide
evidence for: (1) whether Serpina1e derived from non-muscle sources contributes to the
exercise-induced plasma pool of Serpina1e, (2) whether the experimental design for reducing
Serpina1e in skeletal muscle was appropriately optimized, and (3) whether Serpina1e
improves hippocampal memory in the Morris water maze test.
In response to these points, we have improved our manuscript with additional results and
substantial revisions as follows:
1. To detect exercise-induced Serpina1 family proteins derived from non-muscle tissues,
we performed additional LC-MS/MS analysis on plasma proteins remaining after the
depletion of biotinylated proteins. Our results showed that exercise does not
increase the amount of non-muscle-derived Serpina1 family proteins.
2. To address the concern that the exercise training of the S1eKO/EX group was
insufficient for memory enhancement, we compared the exercise intensities of
S1eKO/EX mice to those of exercised control mice (normal Serpina1e in muscles).
Our results showed that the S1eKO/EX mice performed similar amounts of
exercise compared to the control mice.
3. In response to the concern that our lentiviral vector-mediated reduction of muscular
Serpina1e may be non-specific, we measured Serpina1e mRNA levels in lentiviral
vector-injected muscles and other non-injected tissues. Our semi-quantitative RT-
PCR results showed that intramuscular delivery of lentiviral vectors does not
affect Serpina1e expression in other tissues.
4. Because Reviewer #3 suggested that “robust gold-standard assays” such as the
Morris Water Maze (MWM) should be performed for at least some of the key
experiments in our study, we additionally conducted the MWM test after systemic
administration of recombinant Serpina1e. Our results showed that Serpina1e-
administered mice exhibited improved memory performance in the MWM test,
consistent with our findings from the contextual fear conditioning test.
All changes in the text of the revised manuscript have been highlighted in red.
We hope these revisions and additional results adequately address all reviewers’ points and
strengthen our findings on muscle-derived Serpina1e mediating exercise-induced cognitive
enhancement. We believe that this revised manuscript is suitable for publication in Nature
Communications.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
I thank the authors for considering my points and for revising the text accordingly. However, it seems that no new experiments were done to address the outstanding issues. Therefore, I remain skeptical of the overall conclusions of this manuscript as they are not fully supported by the analyses. In particular, I remain not convinced that the skeletal muscle is a significant source of circulating Serpina1e even after exercise because this circulating factor is more highly (>100x) expressed in other organs (such as the liver) and therefore it seems unlikely that the muscle pool would significantly impact the circulating levels of Serpina 1e.
While I understand there are limitations of the TurboID approach, the authors have previously utilized mass spectrometry to measure Serpina 1e levels in the circulation. Therefore, the authors could utilize this approach to define how much Serpina 1e is secreted by muscle vs. other organs by measuring Serpina 1e levels in the mice with muscle-targeted knockdown of Serpina 1e compared to controls. This approach is independent of TurboID and, therefore, I do not see any technical limitations in applying it to determine what proportion of circulating Serpina 1e is secreted by muscle in control conditions and following exercise.
Altogether, without addressing experimentally this issue, it remains unclear whether muscle-secreted Serpina 1e is a meaningful contributor to the circulating pool of Serpina 1e.
Likewise, I remain unconvinced that Serpina 1e knockdown in muscle abrogates the protective effects of exercise on the brain as claimed by the authors because there are many circulating factors (secreted by muscle and other tissues) such as irisin and cathepsin B that have been reported to exert this function. Therefore, I find it odd that Serpina 1e knockdown would completely abrogate the positive effects of exercise on memory, as found by the authors.
“We found that S1eKO/EX mice showed no enhancement in memory retrieval in the NOR and CFC tests (Fig. 4k, l) and no positive correlation between running distance and memory performance (Supplementary Fig. 17i)”.
Altogether, I find this manuscript interesting but several conclusions are based on suboptimal or incomplete experiments. While I suggested a few key analyses that would have mitigated these outstanding issues, the authors have not provided any new data to address these points despite standard experimental approaches (e.g. mass spec) available for these analyses. Therefore, I remain unconvinced about the overall robustness and validity of this study.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Responses to the REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
I thank the authors for their work in addressing my queries. While I appreciate their efforts,
the pressing questions I previously asked have been answered only in part. Therefore, I
would please request the authors to address these remaining points:
(1) Please clearly define what % of the circulating Serpina 1e derives from the skeletal
muscle versus other tissues in control conditions and in response to exercise. To this
purpose, you can utilize the LC-MS/MS mass spec approach you previously used for the
analysis of immunoprecipitated biotinylated proteins, which are muscle-derived, vs.
leftover fractions, which consist of proteins secreted from other tissues. Please display
the resulting data on the same graph so that it is possible to appreciate whether the
skeletal muscle contributes a meaningful amount of Serpina 1e in control conditions
and/or following exercise compared to other tissues. Without this analysis, it remains
unclear whether muscle-secreted Serpina 1e is a significant contributor to the circulating
pool of Serpina 1e. Please clearly define what % of the circulating Serpina 1e derives from
the skeletal muscle compared to other tissues.
: We thank the reviewer for this excellent question. Defining the relative contribution of different
tissues to the circulating Serpina1e pool is a critical step in understanding its systemic function.
We fully agree that this information would further clarify the tissue origin of circulating Serpina1e.
However, accurately quantifying the relative contribution of skeletal muscle versus other tissues
to the circulating Serpina1e pool is currently not feasible due to inherent limitations of in vivo
proximity labeling systems, including the TurboID system. As the reviewer requested, this would
require comparing the biotinylated (muscle-derived) protein to the non-biotinylated (non-muscle-
derived) fraction. However, this comparison would not produce biologically meaningful results for
two main reasons:
1. Low and unknown labeling efficiency: The biotinylation efficiency of TurboID and the
detection of biotinylated proteins are known to be very low and inconsistent even under
optimal conditions due to the several factors, such as expression level of proximity labeling
enzyme, efficiencies of protein biotinylation and enrichment of biotinylated proteins,
and dynamic range of LC-MS (Qian et al., 2006, Molecular & Cellular Proteomics 5: 1727–
1744; Kim et al., 2014, Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A, 111(24):E2453-61; Branon et al., 2018,
Nat Biotechnol., 36, 880–898; Cho et al., 2020, Nat Protoc., 15, 3971–3999; Jiang et al.,
2024, ACS Meas Sci Au., 4: 338-417; Yang et al., 2024, bioRxiv
12.17.628942; doi: https://doi.org/10.1101/2024.12.17.628942).
In addition, it has been reported that biotinylation efficiency of TurboID is relatively low in
specific cellular compartments like the ER, where Serpina1e is processed for secretion
(Branon et al., 2018, Nat Biotechnol., 36, 880–898; Cho et al., 2020, Nat Protoc., 15,
3971–3999). Taken together, these suggest that our system cannot exactly determine
what fraction of muscle-derived Serpina1e is actually labeled in vivo.
2. Confounding analytic variables: Quantitative comparison would be confounded by
inconsistent variables, such as in vivo biotin delivery kinetics and the limited labeling
radius of the TurboID enzyme (Kim et al., 2014, Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A, 111(24): E2453-
61; Qian et al., 2006, Molecular & Cellular Proteomics 5: 1727–1744). Therefore, these
inconsistent and uncontrollable variables would render any ratiometric comparison
between the labeled and unlabeled fractions unreliable.
While these technical issues prevent us from calculating an exact percentage of muscle-derived
Serpina1e in the systemic pool, our data already provide indirect yet compelling evidence
addressing the reviewer's core question, whether skeletal muscle represents a significant source
of circulating Serpina1e. We demonstrated that:
- A muscle-derived pool of biotinylated Serpina1e becomes detectable in the circulation
following exercise (Fig. 2 and 3).
- Limb muscles exhibited elevated Serpina1e mRNA following exercise (Supplementary Fig.
17f), despite lower baseline expression than in the liver.
- Muscle-specific Serpina1e knockdown (Supplementary Fig. 17f) abolishes both the exercise-
induced increase in the intramuscular Serpina1e transcript and associated enhancements in
hippocampal memory (Fig. 4k, l) and neurogenesis (Fig. 6g, h).
Taken together, these findings clearly indicate that skeletal muscle is a physiologically relevant
and functionally essential source of circulating Serpina1e in response to exercise.
In summary, although our proximity labeling approach is powerful for specifically identifying
proteins originating from muscle, it is not a quantitative tool for determining their absolute
proportion in circulation. Nonetheless, our data demonstrate that skeletal muscle is a significant
source of a circulating, exercise-responsive pool of Serpina1e, which is the central conclusion
relevant to our study.
We believe that accurately quantifying the contributions of muscle-derived Serpina1e to the
systemic pool may be possible if Serpina1e-specific antibodies or other precise quantitative
protein labeling tools become available in future studies.
In response to the reviewer’s point, we have included the limitations of the TurboID-based
proximity labeling technique as below:
line 322-330: Additionally, the in vivo labeling efficiency of TurboID is relatively low 36 and is inherently
influenced by the subcellular localization of both the enzyme and its target proteins 18. In
our model, TurboID was targeted to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) of skeletal muscle cells,
thereby preferentially labeling proteins that transit through or reside within the ER lumen.
Consequently, cytosolic or non-classically secreted myokines, such as Irisin and Cathepsin
B—which may bypass the conventional ER-Golgi secretion pathway—are unlikely to be
biotinylated and thus could not be detected in our system. Furthermore, even for proteins
processed through the classical secretory pathway like Serpina1e, the inherent limitations
of TurboID can lead to incomplete labeling. This reduces detection sensitivity and precludes
reliable quantitative measurements in vivo.
We also emphasize that the skeletal muscle is the essential source of exercise-induced Serpina1e
in the Discussion part of the revised manuscript as below:
line 336-338: Despite the dominant expression in the liver 29,36, our data demonstrate a muscle-specific
upregulation following exercise, both at the mRNA and protein level (Fig. 2 and 3;
Supplementary Fig. 8 and 9) after 4 weeks of wheel running exercise.
(2) Please utilize the same mass spec approach as above to better characterize the
lentiviral model of Serpina1e knockdown. Specifically, the authors should measure the
circulating levels of Serpina1e in mice with or without Serpina1e knockdown in control
conditions and following exercise. Also in this case, the data for all conditions should be
displayed on the same graph.
: We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to further characterize our knockdown model at the
protein level. While we agree that measuring circulating Serpina1e following knockdown would
be of interest, we respectfully argue that our existing data provide a definitive validation of the
functional relevance of our knockdown model for two key reasons:
1. Technical limitations of detecting a partial reduction in circulating Serpina1: As discussed
in our previous response, accurately quantifying total circulating Serpina1e via LC-MS is
technically challenging. Detecting a modest reduction in circulating Serpina1e, resulting
from a partial knockdown in muscles, would likely fall below the sensitivity and reliability
threshold of this method. These technical limitations would make the measurement
potentially inconclusive and difficult to interpret.
2. Conclusive validation of knockdown via functional outcomes: The validity of our
knockdown model is best demonstrated by its clear biological consequences. Our data
show that a significant reduction of Serpina1e mRNA at the source (Fig. 4i; Supplementary
Fig. 17e, f), a well-established indicator of knockdown efficacy, is accompanied by a
marked loss of the cognitive benefits of exercise and its associated neurogenesis (Fig. 4k,
l; Fig. 6g, h). This direct link between local transcript loss and the impairment in systemic
functions provides compelling evidence for the critical role of muscle-derived Serpina1e.
In summary, we acknowledge the importance of protein-level quantification for addressing the
exact contribution of muscle-derived Serpina1e to the systemic pool. However, we believe the
functional consequences observed following Serpina1e knockdown provide more robust and
biologically meaningful validation of the role of Serpina1e, rather than a technically challenging
measurement that may not be reliable.
(3) I am not convinced that lentiviral injection in the limbs will target all limb muscles and
represent a knockdown of Serpina 1e in 73-75% of all body muscles as claimed by the
authors. This is unlikely because major muscles such as the diaphragm are not targeted
and because the limb injection that the authors do is most likely an intramuscular injection
that delivers the virus primarily to only one limb muscle, whereas the other limb muscles
remain most likely untargeted. The authors should test whether indeed all limb muscles
are targeted by doing a qRT-PCR for Serpina1e from each of the individually dissected
limb muscles, western blots for Serpina1 from dissected limb muscles, and/or mass spec.
: We thank the reviewer for insightful concerns regarding the extent and validation of our lentiviral
knockdown model.
First, to clarify a key point, our manuscript does not claim a knockdown in '73-75% of all body
muscles.' Our goal was to achieve a functionally significant knockdown in the large limb muscles,
which are the primary effectors in our exercise model.
Second, while we understand the request for analyzing individual muscle with qRT-PCR,
western blot, or mass spec to validate comprehensive knockdown efficacy across all limb muscles,
we respectfully disagree that this level of detail is essential for validating the core conclusions of our
study.
1. Contribution of untargeted muscles is negligible:
As the reviewer pointed out, the diaphragm or other muscle was not targeted by the lentiviral
vector in our study. However, its contribution to total body muscle is negligible.
In case of normal human adults, the average weight of the diaphragm is approximately 200 g,
accounting for about 3 to 4% of body weight (e.g., Thurlbeck, 1978, Thorax, 33: 483-487). Given
that skeletal muscles comprise approximately 40% of total body weight (e.g., Frontera and Ochala,
2015, Calcif Tissue Int. 96: 183-195), the diaphragm's mass constitutes only about 1% of total
muscle mass. It appears that rodents have a similar or even smaller proportion of diaphragm
mass. Therefore, any contribution from the diaphragm or similar size of the muscle to the exercise-
induced pool of Serpina1e is expected to be insignificant compared to the large limb muscles we
targeted.
2. Widespread transduction of lentiviral vectors in limb muscles is well-established:
Regarding the concern about localized delivery, we respectfully disagree that injection targets
only a single muscle.
The intramuscular injection of viral vectors is a well-established technique for achieving
transduction of foreign genes in multiple muscle fibers. Given our conditions for injecting the
lentiviral vector (5 x 10^8 TU / 25 µL per limb), it is highly likely that the injected lentiviral vectors
spread and transduced a wider region of the limb musculature around the injected sites. Previous
studies have demonstrated that lentiviral particles can transduce multiple adjacent muscles after
a single intramuscular injection (e.g., O'Rourke et al., 2003, Mol. Ther., 7: 632-639; Talbot et al.,
2009, Mol. Ther., 18: 601-608; Kimura et al., 2009, Mol. Ther., 18(1): 206-213). We used similar
ranges of viral titer and volume for our intramuscular injection of the lentiviral vector.
3. Validation of our lentiviral knockdown model with functional outcome:
Our primary objective was to investigate the impact of lowering Serpina1e expression on exercise-
induced cognitive enhancement. The validity of our knockdown model is best demonstrated by its
biological impact: the lentiviral vector-mediated knockdown resulted in a significant reduction
of Serpina1e transcripts in limb muscle, leading to the complete abolishment of cognitive and
neurogenic benefits of exercise (Fig. 4h-l, Fig. 6g, h, Supplementary Fig. 17).
In summary, the definitive functional outcome of our knockdown experiments provides the most
critical validation of our lentiviral Serpina1e knockdown in skeletal muscles. Our functional
evidence, combined with the quantitative insignificance of untargeted muscles, provides a robust
and reliable basis for our conclusions. While individual muscle analysis would provide a more
detailed and through assessment, it is unlikely to alter the overall conclusion that reducing
Serpina1e levels in skeletal muscle diminishes the effect of exercise on cognitive functions.
(4) The Morris Water Maze results are interesting but preliminary because they are done
with a low number of animals (n=5-7). Normally, a higher number of animals is used in
behavioral tests like this to ensure the robustness and reproducibility of the findings.
: We acknowledge the reviewer’s concern regarding the limited sample size used in the Morris
water maze (MWM) test. To minimize animal sacrifice while maintaining statistical rigor, we
employed a relatively small cohort of mice for the behavioral assessments. In the revised
manuscript, we have designated the MWM results as ‘preliminary’ to reflect this limitation.
However, we would like to emphasize that these findings are in line with the significant
improvements in memory performance in other behavioral tests. Our MWM results demonstrate
a trend consistent with findings from contextual fear conditioning (Fig. 4a, b). Furthermore, an
alternative approach to increase the systemic Serpina1e level – intramuscular overexpression of
Serpina1e – also yielded significant improvements in memory performance in the novel object
recognition and contextual fear conditioning tests (Fig. 4c-e). Therefore, we believe that
increasing the number of animals in the MWM would not substantially alter these consistent
findings.
The description of our findings were revised as below:
line 197~201: Sedentary mice administered recombinant Serpina1e exhibited improved performance in the
CFC test (Fig. 4b; Supplementary Fig. 11), while Serpina1a had no such effect
(Supplementary Fig. 13). Our preliminary results from the MWM test (Supplementary Fig.
12) also demonstrated a consistent improvement in spatial memory performance following
the administration of recombinant Serpina1e.
(5) There are many factors secreted by skeletal muscle following exercise that contribute
to increasing cognitive capacity (e.g. irisin and cathepsin B), in addition to exercise-
induced signals secreted by other tissues (such as the liver) that similarly improve
cognition. Therefore, I find it odd that Serpina 1e knockdown would completely abrogate
the positive effects of exercise on memory, as found by the authors: “We found that
S1eKO/EX mice showed no enhancement in memory retrieval in the NOR and CFC tests
(Fig. 4k, l) and no positive correlation between running distance and memory performance
(Supplementary Fig. 17i)”.
: As the reviewer pointed out, there are known myokines, such as FNDC5/irisin and Cathepsin B,
as well as other exercise-induced factors (“exerkines”) that have been shown to improve cognitive
function.
While our data demonstrated the essential role of muscle-derived Serpina1e in exercise-induced
cognitive functions, we did not exclude the possibility that other exerkines play a role in cognitive
enhancement. In the Discussion of the previous version of the manuscript (line 343~349), we
already suggest that Serpina1e may share downstream signaling with other myokine such as
Irisin. We now extend this point by providing additional explanations as below:
The beneficial effects of exercise on cognitive functions appear to be mediated by the complex
and cooperative actions of multiple exerkines rather than by the individual effect of a single
exerkine. This is because intense and chronic physical activities trigger systemic interactions
among various organs, including muscles, liver, bone, and adipose tissue (Severinsen et al.,
2020, Endocrine Reviews, 41(4): 594-609).
In fact, elevations in BDNF levels, neurogenesis, and neurite growth by Serpina1e are common
physiological consequences of exerkines in the hippocampus. These functional similarities
between Serpina1e and other exerkines raise the possibility that exercise-induced changes in
brain function are mediated by the cooperative functions of multiple exerkines.
For instance, lactate produced during intense exercise can be transported to the hippocampus,
resulting in the upregulation of BDNF expression through SIRT1-PGC1a signaling (Hayek et al.,
2019, J. Neurosci., 39(13): 2369–2382). This lactate-induced BDNF was mediated
by PGC1a/FNDC5 pathway, suggesting that the beneficial effects of exercise on cognitive
functions are dependent on complex interactions among multiple exerkine-related signaling
pathways. Additionally, the anti-inflammatory functions of Serpina1e may correlate with those of
other myokines, such as irisin, because irisin can suppress glial activation and inflammatory
signaling in the diseased brain (Islam et al., 2021, Nat. Metab., 3: 1058-1070; Peng et al.,
2017, Mol. Immunol., 91: 185-194). While the molecular identities of exerkines that functionally
interact with Serpina1e remain unclear, it is possible that Serpina1e plays a crucial role as either
an upstream or downstream signaling component essential for exerkine-induced cognitive
enhancement.
Therefore, our data showing no exercise-induced cognitive enhancement or related changes in
the hippocampus following Serpina1e knockdown suggest that Serpina1e is an essential
component for the exercise-induced modulation of cognitive functions. Moreover, the beneficial
effects of other exerkines on cognitive functions appear to depend on Serpina1e-related signaling.
In our future studies, we will explore whether Serpina1e signaling interacts with other exercise-
induced factors and how Serpina1e interacts with other exerkines during exercise-induced
cognitive enhancements.
In response to the reviewer’s feedback, we strengthened our discussion on the potential
interaction between Serpina1e and other exercise-induced factors in the Discussion section of
the revised manuscript, as below:
line 354~378: The beneficial effects of exercise on cognitive functions may be mediated by the complex
and cooperative actions of multiple exerkines, rather than by the individual effect of a single
exerkine. Exercise triggers systemic interactions among various organs, including muscles,
liver, bone, and adipose tissue. Indeed, the elevations in BDNF levels, neurogenesis, and
neurite growth induced by Serpina1e (Fig. 6) are common physiological consequences
shared among various exerkines, raising the possibility that exercise-induced changes in
brain function are mediated by a cooperative functional network. This potential cooperation
is exemplified by the functional overlap between Serpina1e and Irisin, both of which
increase the number of newborn neurons and the expression of BDNF. Moreover, a recent
study indicated a possible overlap in the downstream signaling pathways of Serpina1 and
Irisin. Serpina1 proteins interacts with Ephrin type-B receptor 2 (EphB2) to promote cell
proliferation and improve thermogenesis and glucose metabolism by the uncoupling protein
1 (UCP1) 29. Meanwhile, Irisin also upregulates browning-associated genes and UCP1
protein in cultured adipocytes and adipose tissues 38. Additionally, the anti-inflammatory
functions of Serpina1e may correlate with those of other myokines, such as irisin, because
irisin can suppress glial activation and inflammatory signaling in the diseased brain 39,40.
Crosstalk among multiple exerkine pathways is further highlighted by findings that lactate,
produced during intense exercise, can upregulate BDNF expression through
PGC1a/FNDC5 signaling 41. Therefore, the abolishment of exercise-induced cognitive
enhancement by muscle Serpina1e knockdown (Fig. 4k, l; Supplementary Fig. 17i) and
related hippocampal changes (Fig. 6g, h) not only indicates that Serpina1e is essential for
the exercise-induced upregulation of hippocampal functions but also suggests that the
beneficial effects of other exerkines depend on Serpina1e-related signaling. Although the
molecular identities of exerkines that functionally interact with Serpina1e remain unclear,
it is plausible that Serpina1e plays a crucial role as either an upstream or downstream
signaling component within this complex exerkine crosstalk.
Responses to the reviewer’s points:
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
o I thank the authors for considering my points and for revising the text accordingly. However,
it seems that no new experiments were done to address the outstanding issues. Therefore, I
remain skeptical of the overall conclusions of this manuscript as they are not fully
supported by the analyses. In particular, I remain not convinced that the skeletal muscle is
a significant source of circulating Serpina1e even after exercise because this circulating
factor is more highly (>100x) expressed in other organs (such as the liver) and therefore it
seems unlikely that the muscle pool would significantly impact the circulating levels of
Serpina 1e.
While I understand there are limitations of the TurboID approach, the authors have
previously utilized mass spectrometry to measure Serpina 1e levels in the circulation.
Therefore, the authors could utilize this approach to define how much Serpina 1e is secreted
by muscle vs. other organs by measuring Serpina 1e levels in the mice with muscle-targeted
knockdown of Serpina 1e compared to controls. This approach is independent of TurboID
and, therefore, I do not see any technical limitations in applying it to determine what
proportion of circulating Serpina 1e is secreted by muscle in control conditions and
following exercise.
Altogether, without addressing experimentally this issue, it remains unclear whether
muscle-secreted Serpina 1e is a meaningful contributor to the circulating pool of Serpina 1e.
- We thank the reviewer for the constructive feedback. We agree that the question of
whether skeletal muscle contributes meaningfully to circulating Serpina1e is
important.
Below we provide three lines of evidence that clarify this point:
(1) High transcript abundance of Serpina1e does not equate to high Serpina1e
protein secretion from the liver
While Serpina1e transcripts are indeed more abundant in the liver than in skeletal
muscle (for the very recent example, Okagawa et al., 2024, Nat. Commun., 15:9585),
proteomic studies show that transcript abundance does not necessarily equate to
amount of systemic secretion.
For example, studies employing the in situ secretory protein labeling using the ER-
anchored TurboID approach (Kim et al., 2021, Nature Comm., 12: 5204 and Wei et al.,
2021, Nat Chem Biol., 17: 326-334) demonstrated liver-secreted proteins but failed
detect Serpina1e among circulating liver-derived proteins, although other
Serpina1 proteins were detected.
This result indicates that liver-derived Serpina1e protein in the plasma is not well
correlated with its high transcript abundance. The similar poor correlation between
mRNA and protein expression has widely been observed in diverse cell types (for
example, Nusinow et al., 2020, Cell, 180: 387-402).
Furthermore, a recent organism-wide secretome atlas (Wei et al., 2023, Cell Metab.,
35: 1261-1279) also support the notion that the liver is not a dominant source of
circulating Serpina1e. In this dataset, Serpina1e was identified as a secretory protein
from multiple tissues, including both liver and skeletal muscle. Our quantitative re-
analysis of these data shows that relative contributions of liver and muscle to the
circulating Serpina1e are comparable under sedentary conditions (below Figure 1).

(3) No increase in the non-muscle-derived Serpina1e protein following exercise
Our streptavidin-based fractionation of biotinylated- and non-biotinylated proteins in
plasma of ACTuR mice showed that only the biotinylated (muscle-derived) Serpina1
protein (Serpina1a-e) fraction increased in plasma after exercise, while the non-
biotinylated fraction (leftover) remained unchanged (Fig. 3d, e in the revised
manuscript).
In direct response to the reviewer’s suggestion, we further conducted additional LC-
MS/MS analysis on the non-biotinylated fraction (the biotinylated fraction was
already analyzed in Fig. 2 of the original manuscript) during the previous round of
revision.
These additional results confirmed that Serpina1e level in the non-biotinylated fraction
did not change following exercise (Supplementary Fig. 10 in the revised
manuscript).
Please see Fig. 2 below for direct comparison of Serpina1e levels in the biotinylated
and non-biotinylated fractions.
Figure 2. Serpina1e level in plasma of ACTuR mouse analyzed by LC-MS/MS
a. Serpina1e level in the biotinylated fraction of the plasma (secreted from skeletal muscles,
adapted from Fig. 2 in the original manuscript).
b. Serpina1e level in the non-biotinylated fractioin of the plasma (secreted from non-skeletal
muscles, adapted from Supplementary Fig. 10 in the revised manuscript).
Taken together, these independent in vivo secretome-mapping studies as well as our
findings provide strong orthogonal support for our conclusion that skeletal muscle is
the physiologically relevant source of circulating Serpina1e.
o Likewise, I remain unconvinced that Serpina1e knockdown in muscle abrogates the
protective effects of exercise on the brain as claimed by the authors because there are many
circulating factors (secreted by muscle and other tissues) such as irisin and cathepsin B that
have been reported to exert this function. Therefore, I find it odd that Serpina 1e knockdown
would completely abrogate the positive effects of exercise on memory, as found by the
authors. Furthermore, it seems unlikely the authors’ claim that the activity of cathepsin B
and irisin (and of any other exercise-induced protective factor, secreted by muscle and other
tissues) would strictly depend on optimal Serpina 1e levels.
- We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding the dominant role of
Serpina1e in mediating cognitive benefits of exercise.
As pointed by the reviewer, other exercise-induced myokines, including FNDC5/Irisin
and Cathepsin B, have been shown to be required for promoting hippocampal memory.
However, given evidence from our work and other studies, these results are thought
to be due to the mechanisms that exercise-induced myokines may act cooperatively
rather than independently.
(1) Interdependent actions of myokines in exercise-induced cognitive benefits
Previous studies have demonstrated that the genetic deletion of Fndc5 (Islam et al.,
2023, Nat. Metab., 5:1058–1070) or Ctsb (Moon et al., 2018, Cell Metab., 24:332–340)
leads to an impairment in exercise-induced memory enhancement, even though other
myokines presumably remain intact.
These findings, along with our results, raise the possibility that multiple exercise-
induced myokines functionally interact to support cognitive benefits, and that disruption
of any key component can attenuate the overall effect of myokines.
(2) New data suggesting a functional Serpina1e-Fndc5 interaction
To test whether Serpina1e influences other myokines associated with cognitive
enhancement, we conducted additional experiments.
Our new results showed that Serpina1e regulates the Fndc5 expression in
skeletal muscle (Fig. 3 below):
(a) AAV-mediated overexpression of Serpina1e in skeletal muscle (S1eOE)
modestly increased Fndc5 levels
(b) Conversely, lentiviral knockdown of Serpina1e in skeletal muscle (S1eKO)
significantly reduced Fndc5 levels
(c) These effects were selective, because Ctsb expression remained
unchanged under both conditions.
Together, these findings suggest that Serpina1e acts as a functional upstream
regulator of Fndc5 in skeletal muscle, providing a plausible mechanistic explanation
for why Serpina1e knockdown abolishes the cognitive benefits of exercise.
In conclusion, these findings collectively support the notion that exercise-induced
cognitive enhancement depends on a coordinated functional network of multiple
myokines—as exemplified by the Serpina1e–FNDC5 axis in this study—rather than a
single independent signaling pathway.

o Altogether, I find this manuscript interesting but several conclusions are based on

reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
The authors have performed an additional experiment (Figure 4) to address my original query whether Serpina1e is responsible/required for the exercise-induced enhancement in cognition. To address this they have reduced S1e expression in muscle tissue using a lentiviral strategy. Here they show that there is no significant difference in cognitive function between the control, S1eKO and the S1e+ exercice mice and they conclude that this supports the conclusion that muscle-derived Serpina1e mediates exercise-induced cognitive enhancement. The data however, showing that this exercise paradigm leads to enhancement in in NORT and CFCT in these mice is absent. It is hard to determine whether the effect of exercise on cognition is blocked by the knockdown or is absent.
The authors have also added in additional neurogenesis quantification in Figure 6. I query why only a n=3 mice were phenotyped for BrdU/NeuN (Fig 6e,f), when there were BrdU counts for 6-7 mice per group in panel D. This is a very small N.
To assess dendritic arborization, the authors have measured MAP2 intensity as a proxy of dendritic complexity. It would have been much more informative to make measures from individual neurons from each group of mice to assess parameters such as dendritic length, number of branches etc.
