Intramuscular injection of AAV9 and lentiviruses
To investigate whether muscular Serpina1e elicits cognitive enhancement, we delivered a single dose of AAV9-CMV-Serpina1e-T2A-EGFP (VectorBuilder; 1.06 × 10e11 GCs/mouse) into each of the four limbs of C57BL/6 mice. For the control mice, the same dose of AAV9-CMV-EGFP (VectorBuilder; 1.07 × 10e11 GC/mouse) was used instead. In addition, to evaluate whether muscular Serpina1e promotes neuronal outgrowth, the same strategies using AAVs were used to Thy1-EGFP mice. Behavioral assessments and morphological were performed four weeks after viral infection.
To examine whether the role of muscle-derived Serpina1e on exercise-induced beneficial effects, we intramuscularly single injected LV-hCas9:T2A:Puro-U6>Serpina1egRNA1-U6>Serpina1egRNA2 (VectorBuiler; 5 x 10e6 TU/mouse) to reduce the Serpina1e expression in skeletal muscle into four limbs. For the control mice, the same dose of LV-EGFP:T2A:Puro-EF1a>mCherry (VectorBuiler; 5 x 10e6 TU/mouse) was used. Behavioral assessments started two weeks after viral infection.

Infusion of Serpina1e into the hippocampus
To address the direct effects of Serpina1e treatment on the hippocampus, we infused Serpina1e into the molecular layer of the hippocampus (AP -1.95, ML ±1.20, and DV -1.70; Supplementary Fig. 19e) with the same timeline as systemic injections. A custom dual-guide cannula was designed with a 26-gauge, 7.8 mm pedestal height, 2.4 mm distance and 2 mm distance below the pedestal (RWD). The dual-guide cannula was implanted and covered with a dummy cannula with a 1 mm projection to fit the dual-guide cannula. A total of 100 ng/250 nl of Serpina1e per hemisphere was infused through the implanted cannula for 4 weeks every 3 days at 100 nl/min. The actual infused site in the hippocampus was determined by injecting DiI dye through the implanted cannula when all behavioral tests had concluded.

Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays of BDNF
To measure BDNF levels in the hippocampus, C57BL/6 mice were intravenously injected with Serpina1e for 4 weeks every 3 days and then sacrificed 1 hour after the last injection. Hippocampal tissues were harvested following perfusion with PBS and lysed with lysis buffer (1% Triton X-100, 0.1% Tween 20, 100x P.I.C., and 1x PBS). The BDNF concentration was determined via enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (Novusbio) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Cell culture
Cell line culture AML12 cell (ATCC) which is a hepatocyte cell line derived from a liver of mouse was cultured in normal medium (10% FBS (Thermo Scientific), 5,000 U/ml penicillin and 5,000 µg/ml streptomycin in DMEM (Gibco)) for Serpina1e knockdown efficiency tests in vitro. The cell line was authenticated by its supplier (ATCC) and not tested for mycoplasma contamination.
Primary cortical neuron culture Cortical neurons were prepared from the brains of C57BL/6 embryos at embryonic days 16-17. Cortices were dissected in dissection medium (10 mM HEPES in HBSS, Gibco), incubated in 0.25% trypsin-EDTA (Gibco) in a 37°C water bath for 20 min, and then triturated with 2 ml of plating medium (2 mM L-glutamine (Gibco), 0.45% glucose (Sigma‒Aldrich), 10% FBS (Thermo Scientific), 5,000 U/ml penicillin and 5,000 µg/ml streptomycin in MEM (Gibco)). Dissociated cells were filtered through a cell strainer and plated on poly-L-lysine-coated coverslips in 12-well plates (3 × 105 cells/well) in plating media. After one hour, the plates were replaced with maintenance medium (2% B27 supplement, Thermo Scientific), 2 mM L-glutamine, 5,000 U/ml penicillin and 5,000 µg/ml streptomycin in neurobasal medium (Gibco).

Acquisition and analysis of fluorescence images
Immunofluorescence images were obtained, quantified, and analyzed by an observer who was blinded to the treatment. To validate TurboID-ER expression in ER in skeletal muscle, fluorescence images were acquired by using a STELLARIS 8 microscope (Leica, 100x/1.40 NA) with the pinhole set to 1 Airy unit. For neurogenesis analysis via BrdU staining, fluorescence images were acquired by using a STELLARIS 8 microscope (Leica, 40x/1.10 NA) with the pinhole set to 1 Airy unit. Images were taken at the suggested optimal value interval based on magnification and analyzed using ImageJ (National Institutes of Health). Six series of DG slices (290.77 µm x 290.77 µm at intervals of 120 µm) from the dorsal hippocampus of each hemisphere (12 sections per mouse) were selected and the number of BrdU-labeled cells was manually counted.
For neurite analysis using MAP2 staining, Z-stack images of MAP2-positive dendrites (775.19 µm x 775.19 µm x 7 µm) were acquired by using a STELLARIS 8 microscope (Leica, 20x/0.75 NA) with the pinhole set to 1 Airy unit and zoom factor 0.75x. 2D-projected with maximum intensity was measured to compare the complexity of dendrites, represented by MAP2 intensity, between control and muscle Serpina1e-overexpressed mice. For the neurite morphological assessment of individual neurons, sparsely labeled GFP-positive neurons in the hippocampus were imaged using a Leica SP8 confocal microscope (20x/0.75 NA). Z-stacks were acquired with a 2 um z-step for a total of 40 steps, covering a total thickness of 80 um. The acquired z-stacks were processed into maximum intensity projections (MIP). Individual neurons were manually isolated from the MIP images via Region of Interest (ROI) extraction to ensure singular cell analysis. The isolated images were further processed for skeletonization using ImageJ/FIJI. Morphological parameters, including total neurite length and dendritic complexity via Sholl analysis (calculating the number of neurite crossings at intervals of 10 um from the soma), were quantified to evaluate the structural properties of the neurons. To analyze neurite morphology of primary neurons, cortical neurons at DIV7 were used. The neurons were imaged using a Leica SP8 confocal microscope (20x/0.75 NA). The images were processed for skeletonization via ImageJ/FIJI, and the total neurite length, branch number, and branch length were analyzed. The skeletonized images were further analyzed via the Sholl analysis plugin in ImageJ/FIJI, which calculates the number of neurite crossings at intervals of 10 µm from the cell body.

Statistics and Reproducibility
All the statistical analyses were performed via GraphPad Prism 10 with 95% confidence, and all the values are expressed as the mean ± SEM. One-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s post hoc tests was used to compare three or four groups, and unpaired two-tailed Student’s t tests were used to compare two groups. Because the data in Fig. 4k did not pass the normality test, we used a non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis test. The data in Fig. 6n and Supplementary Fig. 20f were analyzed via two-way ANOVA with Sidac’s and Dunnett’s post hoc test, respectively. The statistical tests for each experiment are provided in the legends of the respective figures. P values less than 0.05 were considered statistically significant. All experiments were repeated at least 3 times independently.

Data availability
All data are provided in the Supplementary Information and Source Data file. Source data are provided with this paper. The mass spectrometry proteomics data generated in this study have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE [PMID:34723319] partner repository under the dataset identifier PXD055604. For further inquiries, please contact the Corresponding author.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

This is a sophisticated study involving complex analyses that revealed a novel myokine (Serpina1e) that is influenced by exercise, can cross the blood brain barrier, and beneficially effect cognitive function, hippocampal neurogenesis and BDNF signaling. Strengths of the paper include the rigorous study design, application of advanced methods, and examination of experimental exercise identifying the Serpina1 family proteins along with both systemic and hippocampal delivery of Serpina1e to assess for BBB permeation and molecular mechanisms. The manuscript is novel, timely, and reveals a new and potentially potent mechanism underlying exercise effects on the brain that will be a significant addition to the field (of a similar magnitude as the breakthrough finding of irisin), with important translational and public health implications. However, there are several areas of the paper that require elaboration. Please consider the following comments and suggestions which may help to further strengthen the manuscript.
1. Abstract, Lines 19-20. “The beneficial effects of exercise on cognitive functions appear to be mediated by muscle-derived secretory factors including myokines”. The authors may want to revise to ‘partially mediator’ or include another indicator to demonstrate that this is likely one of multiple pathways by which exercise beneficially effects cognition (e.g., improved cardiometabolic health, psychosocial factors (improved sleep) resulting from exercise that, in turn, improve cognition).
2. Introduction. Lines 40-42. “…the restorative effect of exercise on cognitive function in patients with brain disorders has been suggested.” Consider being a bit more specific to better orient the readers ( e.g., the restorative effect of exercise on cognitive function in normal aging and in patients with neurologic conditions/neurodegenerative disorders has been suggested).
3. Experimental methods appear adequate though reviewers with greater expertise in proteomic profiling and the ACTuR model may be able to comment further.
4. Results. Authors report that the levels of most of the identified myokines (60 of 78 myokines; 123 ~ 77%) significantly increased after exercise. What led the authors to specifically focus on Serpina1 family proteins for the subsequent analysis? The authors nicely discuss Serpina1 proteins on pg. 8 lines 150-154, though further justification would be helpful in understanding the focus on Serpina1 vs. the number of other myokines increased after exercise. (e.g., are the functional roles of the other myokines relatively more well-established, compared to Serpina1 family proteins?)
5. Were other myokines known to be influenced by exercise and related to exercise-induced cognitive enhancement (irisin, cathepsin B) impacted by the experimental exercise paradigm? Though these myokines are not the focus of the paper, given established evidence of their role, this would be helpful to mention in either the main text or supplement to better contextualize the findings. This data may be included in Fig. 2 panel D, but would be beneficial to explicitly state.
6. Do the authors foresee any limitations that should be acknowledged in the discussion? For instance, does the age of the mice limit interpretation or generalizability in any way (e.g., should the study be replicated in aged mice to better ascertain whether these mechanisms vary across the lifespan)?
7. Discussion. Overall, the conclusions are well supported by the evidence. It may be beneficial to include a few sentences relating the findings to recent work involving other core myokines (e.g., consider how the mechanisms of Serapina1 might interact with, amplify, or otherwise relate to other myokines thought to mediate exercise effects on the brain (e.g., irisin, cathepsin B))?
8. There are a handful of very minor grammatical errors throughout (for example, page 8, lines 163-164 "When assessed the relative amount of plasma Serpina1 protein..."). These are easily addressable and do not detract from the quality of the work.

### Reviewer 2

Dear Editor,
The study addresses an important topic by investigating the role of the myokine Serpina1e in exercise-induced memory enhancement through advanced methods, including murine models, biotinylation, and proteomic analysis. I have outlined the primary points for improvement below to enhance the manuscript’s rigor and clarity.
First, I recommend removing numeric citations in the abstract, as they detract from its clarity and independence. The abstract should be self-contained and easily understood without reference numbers.
Second, the discussion section closely aligns with an overly “perfect” narrative of experimental findings. To enhance scientific transparency, the authors should consider including study limitations, particularly concerning the applicability of murine models to human outcomes. Additionally, it would be beneficial for the authors to discuss any data that did not yield significant results, such as the Morris water maze data obtained using four daily trials, a setup that typically reduces sensitivity to subtle cognitive differences. Furthermore, it would be valuable to compare their findings on Serpina1e with other known myokines linked to exercise-induced cognitive benefits, highlighting any relevant similarities and differences.
These suggestions aim to enhance the study’s clarity and robustness, providing greater transparency and critical analysis of the results and methods.

### Reviewer 3

In this interesting manuscript, Kim et al. examine the role of the myokine Serpina 1e in mediating some of the beneficial effects of exercise on the brain. By using a novel mouse model, the authors identify myokines secreted by muscle in response to exercise, which include Serpina 1e. They further report that, like exercise, Serpina 1e improves cognitive functions, as determined by modulating Serpina 1e levels in muscle and by injecting it in the plasma and hippocampus. Overall, this is an interesting manuscript on an important topic. However, there are several major limitations of the current work that decrease the robustness of the study and confidence in the findings.
Major points
1) The authors have generated an ER-targeted turboID mouse model to label myokines en route to be secreted. However, a better characterization of this mouse model is needed to determine whether the turboID indeed localizes to the ER of muscle cells. Moreover, the authors should determine by western blot whether the ER-targeted turboID can be secreted as well. This is an important control because if the ER-targeted turboID is secreted it can then label proteins in the plasma irrespective of their tissue origin.
2) The authors report that several myokines, including Serpina 1a and 1e, are secreted into the plasm in response to exercise. However, it is unclear if these myokines are transcriptionally induced by exercise or, alternatively, whether there is a residing pool of Serpina 1a and 1e that is secreted only in response to exercise. Gene expression analysis, immunostaining, and western blot should be used to characterize the muscle pool of Serpina 1e and how it modulated by exercise.
3) The analysis in Fig. 3 reports that the muscle-secreted pool of Serpina 1e increases in response to exercise whereas the liver pool does not. While this might be true, Serpina 1e and other serpina family members are highly expressed by the liver compared to skeletal muscle and therefore it remains undetermined whether the muscle-secreted Serpina 1e is indeed substantial enough to offset the circulating pool of Serpina 1e, which primarily derives from the liver given that this is the tissue that primarily expresses it. Therefore, the authors should compare on the same western blot membrane the levels of muscle-derived Serpina 1e versus the levels of Serpina 1e that are found in the leftover plasma from the same preparation (obtained as shown in Fig. 3a).
4) On the same line as the point above, the authors should analyze by mass spectrometry the muscle-derived fraction vs. the leftover fraction (as shown in Fig. 3a) to determine whether the exercise-secreted myokines identified in Fig. 2 indeed represent a meaningful contribution to the systemic pool of these circulating factors. This is important because many of the exercise-induced myokines reported by the authors in Fig. 2 are known to be primarily expressed by non-muscle tissues such as the liver. Therefore, it remains unaddressed whether secretion of these factors by skeletal muscle is substantial enough to contribute to the systemic pool.
5) In Fig. 4, the authors utilize AAVs to induce Serpina 1e expression in the skeletal muscle but they should better document whether there is indeed an upregulation of Serpina 1e in the producing skeletal muscle as expected.
6) Throughout the manuscript, there is a wide range of variability in the number of mice utilized for the behavioral assays. Sometimes this number changes even within the same group of experimental animals that are tested in different assays. For example, Fig. 4d is done with n=5 (saline) and n=6 (Serpina 1e) mice but Fig. 4e (which analyzes the same groups of animals but with a different behavioral assay) is done with n=7/group. What is the reason for this change in the number of animals?
7) The number of animals utilized in the behavioral assays seems rather small, also considering the inherent variability of these assays.
8) The assessment of cognitive function is done with novel object recognition and with fear conditioning. However, there are other assays, such as the Morris water maze, listed in the methods but no data with these assays is reported in the figures for Serpina 1e (only a supplementary figure reports positive effects of exercise with this assay). The authors should perform this gold-standard assay for at least one of their models of Serpina 1e modulation.
9) In Fig. 5a, the authors report that V5-tagged Serpina 1e that is retro-orbitally injected can reach the CSF and the hippocampus. However, the authors should also monitor the total levels of Serpina 1e (injected + endogenous) to determine whether the injection of Serpina 1e indeed increases the total levels of Serpina 1e in the CSF and hippocampus. For these studies, they can utilize the anti-Serpina 1 antibody used in Fig. 4f. On the same line, they should also monitor whether exercise modulates the CSF and hippocampal levels of Serpina 1e.
10) In Figure 6, the authors report that Serpina 1e injection increases cell proliferation in the hippocampus and BDNF levels (by 10%). Are there corresponding changes in BDNF protein levels? This looks overall as a minor effect.
11) It is unclear mechanistically how Serpina 1e would modulate BDNF levels, cell proliferation, and neurite outgrowth. What is the receptor mediating the action of Serpina 1e?
12) The statistical analysis does not seem to be always appropriate. For example, the data in Fig. 4b was analyzed by Student’s t-test but there are 2 variables (before and retrieval) for 2 groups (saline and serpina) and therefore should be analyzed by 2-way ANOVA. This applies also to other graphs such as Fig. 4e and Fig. 5g.
Additional points:
13) There is no loading control (such as Ponceau) for the western blot in Fig. 1e.
14) In Fig. 2 the authors report a global increase in myokines in the plasma in response to exercise. However, how is this data normalized to ensure that this is indeed the case?
15) It is unclear what is the control in Fig. 5e-g.
16) The discussion of scientific background is a bit limited. The authors should better discuss studies that have examined communication between the skeletal muscle and the brain.

### Reviewer 4

In this manuscript Kim and colleagues identify Serpina1e as a myokine that is released by muscle into the plasma following 4 weeks of exercise. The also show that delivery of Serpina1e into the plasma, muscle or hippocampus can replicate the hippocampus-associated learning and memory enhancement observed following exercise. Overall, this is a very interesting study. However, several key points should be addressed before this manuscript would be suitable for publication in Nature Communications.
Major questions:
1. The title of the paper states that Serpina1e “mediates” the exercise-induced enhancement of hippocampal memory. Likewise, in the abstract they state that Serpina1e…..”directly” supports long-term memory formation. I disagree that the data presented here shows this. The authors show that Serpina1e is released by muscle after exercise and that Serpina1e delivery can enhance cognition. However, whether Serpina1e is responsible/required for the exercise-induced enhancement in cognition has not been shown. To show this direct relationship, one would for example need to knock out Serpina1e in the muscle and show that exercise can no longer enhance cognition. These statements should all be toned down throughout the manuscript, including the title.
2. The authors state that Serpina1e delivery increases neurogenesis in the hippocampal dentate gyrus. From the data presented in Figure 6 b one is not able to draw this conclusion. BrdU was injected for the last 5 days of prior to perfusion and BrdU+ cells quantified. These BrdU+ cells will be a mixture of proliferating neural precursor cells, immature neurons that may have already become post-mitotic since the first injection 5 days prior, proliferating microglia etc. To be able to quantify adult neurogenesis it would be best to inject BrdU at the start of the experiment and quantify BrdU+NeuN+ double-positive cells. Alternatively, on the available sections a proliferation marker such as Ki67 could be used to quantify the proliferating cells (ideally co-labelled with other markers such as Tbr2 or Sox2) and the immature newborn neurons could be quantified using DCX staining.
Additionally, it is unclear if the BrdU counts presented in Fig 6b are per section or per DG. There is no information in the methods about which sections were stained with BrdU (i.e., a 1 in 6 series through the whole brain or alike). It is stated that cells were counted from 12 sections – how were these sections chosen? The counts state they are # cells/DG and are around 20-30, which if it is BrdU cells per DG I would expect this count to be hundreds from a young mouse.
3. Changes in dendritic arborization could also be assessed in the same mice in the newborn neurons by performing Sholl analysis on DCX+ cells in vivo. This would significantly strengthen the in vitro finding which was performed on embryonic cortical neurons rather than those from the adult hippocampus.
4. Why were only male mice used in the study? This should be stated in the abstract and discussed in the discussion.
Minor points:
1. In the abstract, it is stated that “the beneficial effects of exercise on cognitive function appear to be mediated by muscle-derived secretory factors”. While muscle is certainly an important tissue that exerkines are secreted from, there are many others i.e. hepatokines, adipokines etc.
2. The sentence “Each dot in the graphs represents a tested mouse” is repeated twice at the end of each supplemental figure legend.
3. The discussion section is very brief. There are a lot of discussion points in the results section that could be moved/expanded on in the discussion.

We have not yet tested the age-dependent effects of Serpina1e on cellular and cognitive
changes. By using young adult mice, our study revealed that exercise-induced Serpina1e
is effective for elevating neurogenesis and the expression of BDNF protein, all of which are
hallmarks of exercise-induced effects in the hippocampus. Because both neuronal loss and
decreased BDNF levels in the hippocampus are prominent in the aged brain (Erickson et
al., 2010, J Neurosci, 30(15):5368-75; Fan et al., 2017, Ann Rev Neurosci 40: 251-272),
exercise has been suggested to improve cognitive functions in middle-aged or old mice
(Marlatt et al., 2012, Developmental Neurobiology 72: 943-952; van Praag et al., 2005, J
Neurosci 25: 8680-8685). It is thus possible that Serpina1e-dependent mechanisms, along
with other exercise-induced myokines, play significant roles in the exercise-induced
restoration of age-associated cognitive decline.

: As the reviewer commented, it is possible that Serpina1 may interact with or modify other
exercise-induced myokines, because neurogenesis and BDNF expression are common
consequences of exercise-induced changes in the brain by Serpina1e and/or irisin and
cathepsin B.
However, the differential mechanisms of exercise-induced factors on cognitive functions
cannot be excluded. Exercise is known to increase the plasma levels of anti-inflammatory
peripheral proteins such as Clusterin (Fig. 2d; Supplementary Table 1 in the revised
manuscript), and the migration of such proteins across several physiological barriers to
the brain could reduce neuroinflammatory gene expression (De Miguel, Z. et al. 2021,
Nature 600:494–499). Similarly, human SERPINA1 could possess anti-inflammatory
properties independent of its anti-protease activity (Jonigk et al., 2013, PNAS, 110: 15007-
15012). Because Serpina1e was reported to have no anti-protease activity, which is not
typical of other paralogs (Serpina1a-d), possibly due to a variance in the P1 amino acid in
the reactive center loop (RCL; Forsyth et al., 2003, Genomics 81: 336–345), Serpina1e
may be implicated in exercise-induced anti-inflammatory functions in the brain, resulting in
upregulation of neuronal growth factors, such as BDNF.
On the other hand, the main effector of Irisin is cAMP/PKA-mediated CREB transcription
(Lourenco et al, 2019, Nat. Med. 25:165-175), and CTSB not only act as a lysosomal
protease but also contributes to the cell growth signaling by activating the Wnt and Notch
receptor signaling (Yu et al., 2025, Trends in Molecular Medicine, S1471-4914(24)00343-
5).
Given such differences of myokine-associated signaling, exercise-triggered secretion and
delivery of multiple myokines to the brain may evoke distinct downstream mechanisms, all
of which may concurrently facilitate neurotrophic events in the hippocampus. Whether
these signaling pathways can elicit cognitive enhancement in a cooperative or differential
manner remains to be addressed.

1. I recommend removing numeric citations in the abstract, as they detract from its
clarity and independence. The abstract should be self-contained and easily understood
without reference numbers.
: As the reviewer commented, we deleted all numeric citations in Abstract in the revised
manuscript.

experimental findings. To enhance scientific transparency, the authors should consider

: As the reviewer commented, we have included the limitations of our study in the
Discussion, particularly concerning the applicability of findings from murine models to
human outcomes.
Our study reveals the novel function of Serpina1e in enhancing hippocampal memory.
Unlike the human SERPINA1 gene, the mouse Serpina1 has five different paralogs. One
of the main differences between Serpina1e and SERPINA1 is the reactive center loop (RCL)
domain, which is responsible for the specificity of anti-protease activity (Sanrattana et al.,
2021, Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U. S. A. 118(45):e2108458118). In fact, mouse Serpina1e is
reported to have no anti-protease activity (Paterson et al., 1995, Biochem Biophys Res
Commun, 219(1):64-9), which is atypical of the other paralogs (Serpina1a-d) and human
SERPINA1. This structural difference between the human and mouse Serpina1 genes may
lead to selective and differential effects of human and mouse Serpina1 on neuronal growth
signaling and cognitive enhancements.
However, it is also possible that common structural and functional domains between human
SERPINA1 and mouse Serpina1 are responsible for modulating brain functions, as our
results showed that both human SERPINA1 and mouse Serpina1e can induce neurite
outgrowth in cultured neurons (Fig. 6). Furthermore, human SERPINA1 could possess anti-
inflammatory properties independent of its anti-protease activity (Jonigk et al., 2013, PNAS,
110: 15007-15012), raising the possibility that mouse Serpina1e is also implicated in anti-
inflammatory signaling.
Further studies are thus required to compare the exact molecular features of SERPINA1
and Serpina1e involved in neuronal growth signaling and to dissect their differential effects
on cognitive enhancements.
Reflecting our responses to the reviewer’s comment, the additional statement is now
included in Discussion in the revised manuscript (line 348~353; 369~372).

maze test in Result in the revised manuscript.

Both an increase in the proliferation of neural progenitor cells and BDNF induction are
common consequences of exercise-induced Serpina1e and other myokines. Therefore, it
is possible that Serpina1e and other myokines may share downstream signaling pathways.
However, it is also possible that Serpina1e and other myokines independently and
cooperatively affect neuronal growth signaling. Serpina1e has been reported to
downregulate inflammatory signaling molecules such as TNF-alpha, CXCL1, MHCII, and
Toll-like receptors (Jonigk et al., 2013, PNAS, 110: 15007-15012). In contrast, Irisin can
stimulate cAMP/PKA-mediated CREB-dependent transcription in the brain (Lourenco et al.,
2019, Nat. Med. 25:165-175). Additionally, by reducing unnecessary proteins as a
lysosomal protease, Ctsb can contribute to the cell growth signaling of neural progenitor
cells by activating the Wnt and Notch receptor pathways (Yu et al., 2025, Trends in
Molecular Medicine, S1471-4914(24)00343-5).
Therefore, it is possible that exercise influences cognitive function through multiple
signaling pathways mediated by different myokines. However, whether these myokine-
induced signaling pathways are interconnected or differentially influence cognitive functions
remains to be addressed.

This is important because many of the exercise-induced myokines reported by the

: Our LC-MS/MS method for detecting muscle-derived secretory proteins from ACTuR mice
directly analyzed the enriched fraction of biotinylated proteins (muscle-derived fraction)
from blood plasma (Fig. 2a in the revised manuscript). Therefore, we believe that
additional mass spectrometry of the muscle-derived fraction would be redundant and
unnecessary.
Regarding LC-MS analysis of the leftover plasma fraction, it is well established that plasma
protein concentrations span up to 12 orders of magnitude, with a few abundant proteins
accounting for ~95% of the total plasma proteome, including albumin, which constitutes
more than half of the total protein content (Anderson et al., 2002, Mol. Cell
Proteomics1(11):845-867; Hortin et al., 2006, Clin. Chem. 52(7):1218-1222). Given the
inherent limitations of mass spectrometry and proteomic analyses, these high-abundance
proteins tend to dominate the results, hindering the detection of low-abundance
components (Anderson et al., 2002; Hortin et al., 2006; Hortin et al., 2008, Clin.
Chem. 54(10):1608-1616; Hortin, 2006, Clin. Chem. 52(7):1223-1237). Therefore, we
believe that additional LC-MS analysis of the non-biotinylated plasma fraction would yield
no meaningful insights relevant to our study.
Our results indicate that while many plasma proteins originate from the liver, they are not
exclusively expressed there. It is possible that a smaller fraction of non-liver-derived
proteins contributes to the systemic pool.
Our mass spectrometry method, based on a biotin ligase-mediated protein labeling
technique, has been demonstrated to efficiently identify precise biotinylation sites on
labeled proteins (Shin et al., 2024, Commun Biol. 7:554). Consistent with this, our
proteomics analysis of blood plasma from ACTuR mice detected biotinylated peptides that
are likely derived from skeletal muscle, given the selective expression of TurboID-ER in
muscle (Fig. 1, Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3 in the revised manuscript). By analyzing
the fraction enriched using streptavidin beads, our LC-MS/MS analysis identified 78
putative myokines in plasma, which overlapped significantly with both the mouse plasma
proteome (86%; Fig. 2b) and the skeletal muscle proteome reference datasets (88%; Fig.
2c). Notably, 60 of these 78 putative myokines were significantly increased following
exercise.
Among these 60 exercise-induced myokines, we identified Clusterin (De Miguel et al.,
2021, Nature 600:494-499) and BChe (Horowitz et al., 2020, Science 369(6500):167-173),
both previously reported as exercise-induced plasma proteins. While Clusterin is expressed
ubiquitously with higher levels in the brain, endocrine tissues, liver, and reproductive organs,
BChe is primarily produced in the liver. Our findings indicate that a portion of systemic
Clusterin and BChe induced by exercise originates from muscle tissue.
A similar case applies to Serpina1. While Serpina1 is predominantly expressed in the liver
and lungs, it is also present at lower levels in skeletal muscle. Plasma concentrations
of Serpina1 family proteins were previously reported to increase after six weeks of wheel
running (Horowitz et al., 2020, Science 369:167-173), but the tissue origin of this exercise-
induced increase had not been directly examined.
In our study, Serpina1 family proteins were classified as putative myokines based on our
proteomic analysis. We further detected a significant increase in
biotinylated Serpina1 (muscle-derived due to the muscle-specific expression of ER-
targeted TurboID) in blood plasma from ACTuR mice after four weeks of exercise (Fig. 3
in the revised manuscript). Importantly, this occurred without any exercise-induced
change in total or non-biotinylated (i.e., non-muscle-derived, primarily liver-
derived) Serpina1 levels. Furthermore, our data show that selectively reducing muscle-
derived Serpina1e prevents exercise-induced memory enhancement and neurogenesis
(Fig. 4h~l in the revised manuscript), supporting our conclusion that muscle-
derived Serpina1e plays a key role in exercise-induced brain adaptations.
In summary, given the sensitivity and selectivity of the biotin ligase-based protein labeling
method and the limitations of LC-MS/MS analysis of unlabeled plasma samples, our
approach—leveraging the ACTuR mouse model and LC-MS/MS analysis—effectively
determines the precise tissue origin of circulating secretory proteins in plasma, where
proteins from multiple tissues coexist.
5. In Fig. 4, the authors utilize AAVs to induce Serpina 1e expression in the skeletal
muscle, but they should better document whether there is indeed an upregulation of
Serpina 1e in the producing skeletal muscle as expected.
: As suggested by the reviewer, we provide additional evidence for the AAV-induced
upregulation of Serpina1e mRNA in skeletal muscle. Semi-quantitative RT-PCR analysis of
skeletal muscle tissues (limb muscles) from mice injected with AAVs containing Serpina1e-
EGFP (AAV9-CMV-mSerpina1e:T2A:EGFP; S1eOE) demonstrated that Serpina1e is
significantly overexpressed (~ 350 %), while the expression level of Serpina1a remains
unaffected by AAV injection.
These results are now included in Supplementary Figure 14 of the revised manuscript.
6. Throughout the manuscript, there is a wide range of variability in the number of mice
utilized for the behavioral assays. Sometimes this number changes even within the
same group of experimental animals that are tested in different assays. For example,
Fig. 4d is done with n=5 (saline) and n=6 (Serpina 1e) mice but Fig. 4e (which analyzes
the same groups of animals but with a different behavioral assay) is done with
n=7/group. What is the reason for this change in the number of animals?
: In response to the reviewer’s comment, we re-examined all behavioral data and the
number of mice used in our analyses.
To assess the effect of Serpina1e overexpression (S1eOE) in skeletal muscle on behavior
(Fig. 4c-e), control and S1eOE mice were sequentially subjected to the open field test
(OFT), novel object recognition test (NORT), and contextual fear conditioning test (CFC).
Following the behavioral tests, tissues and plasma fractions from these mice were collected
(Fig. 4g in the revised manuscript).
Initially, each group consisted of seven mice. However, during NORT analysis, two control
mice and one S1eOE mouse were excluded because they did not meet the exploration
time criteria (this was now included in Methods in the revised manuscript, line 601~603),
resulting in a final sample size of control = 5 and S1eOE = 6 for NORT. Since these three
mice exhibited normal behavior in the other tests, their data were retained for OFT and
CFC (control = 7, S1eOE = 7) as well as western blot analysis in the original study.
To prevent any confusion, we have now excluded all behavioral and western blot results
obtained from the mice that did not meet the behavioral analysis criteria. The updated
sample sizes (control = 5, S1eOE = 6) have been corrected in the corresponding figure
legends (figure legend for Fig. 4c-g in the revised manuscript).
7. The number of animals utilized in the behavioral assays seems rather small, also
considering the inherent variability of these assays.
: To minimize unnecessary sacrifice of animals, we aimed to use the minimal number of
mice required for our study. To assess whether our dataset deviated significantly from
normality, we performed a normality test.
Most behavioral datasets followed a normal distribution (see below). However, the dataset
from exercised WT mice expressing lentivirus S1eKO (LV-hCas9:T2A:Puro-U6>gRNA-
U6>gRNA) did not pass the normality test.
Therefore, we used a non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis test to analyze whether the reduced
expression of muscle-derived Serpina1e affects exercise-induced memory enhancement
(Fig. 4l in the revised manuscript).
Despite the limited sample size in the behavioral assays, we observed significant changes
in memory performance following muscle Serpina1e manipulation.
Additionally, we have revised and expanded the details of statistical tests in the Methods
section of the revised manuscript.
8. The assessment of cognitive function is done with novel object recognition and with
fear conditioning. However, there are other assays, such as the Morris water maze,
listed in the methods but no data with these assays is reported in the figures for Serpina
1e (only a supplementary figure reports positive effects of exercise with this assay).
The authors should perform this gold-standard assay for at least one of their models of
Serpina 1e modulation.
: We acknowledge that the Morris water maze is a well-established test for assessing
spatial learning and memory. However, other behavioral tests, such as contextual fear
conditioning (CFC) and novel object recognition (NOR), are also widely recognized
methods for evaluating hippocampus-dependent cognitive functions.
We also observed that skeletal muscle-specific reduction of Serpina1e expression prevents
the exercise-induced improvement in memory retrieval in both the NOR and CFC tests (Fig.
4k, l in the revised manuscript). Furthermore, the same manipulation abolishes the
exercise-induced increase in the number of NeuN/BrdU double-positive cells (Fig. 6g, h in
the revised manuscript).
Therefore, these findings not only highlight the beneficial and essential roles of muscle-
derived Serpina1e in hippocampal memory through the promotion of neurogenesis but also
support the notion that NOR and CFC tests are equally effective as the Morris water maze
in evaluating exercise-modulated hippocampal cognitive functions.
9. In Fig. 5a, the authors report that V5-tagged Serpina 1e that is retro-orbitally injected
can reach the CSF and the hippocampus. However, the authors should also monitor the
total levels of Serpina 1e (injected + endogenous) to determine whether the injection of
Serpina 1e indeed increases the total levels of Serpina 1e in the CSF and hippocampus.
For these studies, they can utilize the anti-Serpina 1 antibody used in Fig. 4f.
: As the reviewer suggested, we attempted to detect changes in total Serpina1e protein
levels (injected + endogenous) in the hippocampus following administration of
recombinant Serpina1e-V5 protein by using anti-Serpina1 antibody targeting.
Consistent with our findings in original study, we detected a significant increase in total
plasma Serpina1 level from mice administered with Serpina1e-V5 (Supplementary Fig.
16d, e in the revised manuscript). Further analysis with CSF collected from mice with
Serpina1e-V5 administration revealed that total Serpina1 is slightly increased
(Supplementary Fig. 16f in the revised manuscript), although western blot analysis with
CSF was not fully replicated due to the limited number of available mice.
We next attempted to detect total Serpina1 level in hippocampal extract from mice with
Serpina1e-V5 administration. Despite some non-specific signals, our western blot results
showed a weak but significant anti-Serpina1 signal in hippocampal extracts from mice
administered with Serpina1e-V5. The detected band matched the expected size of
the Serpina1e-V5 protein and the detected Serpina1 band in plasma (Supplementary Fig.
16d, g-i in the revised manuscript).
Importantly, this corresponding signal was absent in hippocampal extracts from control
(PBS-injected) mice, suggesting that endogenous Serpina1 protein levels in the
hippocampus are negligible or too low to be detected by western blot. This finding aligns
with publicly available data, such as the Human Protein Atlas
(https://www.proteinatlas.org/ENSG00000197249-SERPINA1), which reports that both
mRNA and protein levels of endogenous SERPINA1 are very low in the hippocampus
compared to other tissues.
On the same line, they should also monitor whether exercise modulates the CSF and
hippocampal levels of Serpina 1e.
: As suggested by the reviewer, we attempted several times to detect changes in
total Serpina1 protein levels by performing western blot analysis on hippocampal extracts
using a pan-Serpina1 antibody. However, we were unable to detect any significant signal
corresponding to the expected size of Serpina1 proteins in all groups of mice (please see
the image below).
We suspect that this result is due to the concentration of hippocampus-transmitted
Serpina1(e) being too low to be detected using conventional antibody-based methods such
as western blot. Despite this negative finding, we have already demonstrated that
systemically administered recombinant Serpina1e protein can be detected in the
hippocampus (Fig. 5c,d; Supplementary Fig. 16 in the revised manuscript). This
suggests that Serpina1e is indeed capable of crossing from the bloodstream into the
hippocampus.
10. In Figure 6, the authors report that Serpina 1e injection increases cell proliferation
in the hippocampus and BDNF levels (by 10%). Are there corresponding changes in
BDNF protein levels? This looks overall as a minor effect.
: The BDNF levels shown in Fig. 6c of the original manuscript were measured using an
ELISA assay and directly correspond to BDNF protein levels in the hippocampus. To avoid
any confusion, we will clearly indicate this in the revised manuscript (line 269).
BDNF protein exists at relatively low concentrations, however, even subtle changes in its
levels are known to effectively influence downstream signaling via its high-affinity receptor,
TrkB (Kd ~ 10⁻¹¹ M; Rodrigues-Tebar et al., 1990, Neuron, 4:487-92). Previous studies
have reported that BDNF protein is detectable at 108–256 ng/g of tissue in the
hippocampus, frontal cortex, and neostriatum of the rodent brain (Radka et al., 1996, Brain
Research, 709:122-301). Furthermore, treating cultured hippocampal neurons with as little
as 20 ng/ml of recombinant BDNF is sufficient to elicit BDNF-TrkB-dependent neurite
growth (Righi et al., 2000, J. Neurosci., 20:3165-3174). Additionally, a recent study
demonstrated that even a ~10% change in BDNF levels can alter dendritic growth and
rescue memory impairment induced by hypoxic stress (Li et al., 2025, Sci. Rep., 15:1135).
On the other hand, BDNF secretion and clearance have been reported to occur on the
scale of seconds to minutes (Bergami et al., 2008, JCB, 183:213-221; Han et al., 2021, Sci.
Rep., 11:21203; Park and Poo, 2013, Nat. Rev. Neurosci., 14:7-23), indicating the rapid
and transient kinetics of BDNF concentration in the brain. These unique properties of BDNF
may lead to an underestimation of the extent to which Serpina1 upregulates BDNF when
measured using hippocampal extracts and antibody-based detection methods such as
ELISA.
11) It is unclear mechanistically how Serpina 1e would modulate BDNF levels, cell
proliferation, and neurite outgrowth. What is the receptor mediating the action of
Serpina 1e?
: The receptor for Serpina1e in the brain is totally unknown and remains to be identified. In
peripheral tissues, such as adipocytes, mouse Serpina1 proteins have been reported to
interact with Ephrin type-B receptor 2 (EphB2). This interaction could elicit cell proliferation
and lead to UCP1-induced improvements in thermogenesis and glucose metabolism
(Okagawa et al., 2024, Nature Communications, 15:9585). However, whether EphB2 is
associated with the beneficial effects of Serpina1e on growth signaling has not yet been
examined. Further investigation is required to elucidate the molecular mechanisms
underlying Serpina1e-induced neuronal growth signaling and cognitive enhancement.
We have included additional discussion about the expected downstream signaling of
Serpina1e in the brain in Discussion of the revised manuscript (line 338 ~ 360).
12) The statistical analysis does not seem to be always appropriate. For example,
the data in Fig. 4b was analyzed by Student’s t-test but there are 2 variables (before
and retrieval) for 2 groups (saline and serpina) and therefore should be analyzed by
2-way ANOVA. This applies also to other graphs such as Fig. 4e and Fig. 5g.
: As the reviewer suggested, a two-way ANOVA with Sidak’s post hoc test was used for
contextual conditioning tests in Fig. 4b, 4e, 4l, and 5g in the revised manuscript. Other
data in Supplementary Fig. 10b, 11b, and 12b in the revised manuscript were tested
with a two-way ANOVA with Sidak’s post hoc test.
The change from one-way ANOVA to two-way ANOVA did not result in any changes in the
conclusion of our findings. We have also included detailed information of the statistical
analysis in the Methods of the revised manuscript.
Additional points:
13) There is no loading control (such as Ponceau) for the western blot in Fig. 1e.
: We added ponceau stained membrane image in Fig. 1e in the revised manuscript.
14) In Fig. 2 the authors report a global increase in myokines in the plasma in
response to exercise. However, how is this data normalized to ensure that this is
indeed the case?
: To guide the normalization strategy for LC-MS experiments, we were hinted from Western
blot analysis results.
During Western blot analysis, equal amounts of the plasma fraction acquired from AcTuR
mice were loaded to estimate the total amount of input plasma proteins and the abundance
of biotinylated proteins in plasma. Because the overall intensities of Ponceau staining were
comparable, we assumed that the total input proteins are comparable across all
experimental groups (Fig. 1e, right, in the revised manuscript). However, the levels of
biotinylated proteins were increased in plasma samples from mice provided with biotin, and
the overall amounts of biotinylated proteins were further elevated when exercise was
introduced (Fig. 1e-f in the revised manuscript).
Based on this result, sample preparation for LC-MS/MS analysis was performed with an
equal amount of plasma from each experimental group/mouse as in the Western blot
analysis had been done, to ensure the consistency of the amounts of total plasma proteins.
All samples were processed in parallel to minimize variability and maintain experimental
rigor. When the biotinylated proteome samples were ready, we consistently used the
identical fraction of samples (50% of each sample) for LC-MS/MS analysis, and the
quantification of biotinylated proteins was performed based on label-free quantification
(LFQ) (Cox et al., 2014, Mol. Cell. Proteomics, 13: 2513-2526). Once we obtained the
quantification result of biotinylated proteins, we did not perform any further post-
normalization of the quantified dataset.
Consistent with the Western blot analysis, LC-MS/MS data demonstrated a reproducible
increase in overall biotinylated protein levels upon biotin supplementation, with a further
enhancement observed following exercise combined with biotin supplementation
(Supplementary Fig. 7c in the revised manuscript, ****p<0.0001, one-way ANOVA with
Dunnett’s post hoc test), as shown in Fig. 1e-f in the revised manuscript.
As these two independent experiments showed consistent results, we confirmed that our
observations accurately reflect the actual phenomenon of increased secretion of
biotinylated myokines from muscle upon exercise.
This additional result and description of protein quantification are now updated in
Supplementary Fig. 7 and Methods in the revised manuscript.
15) It is unclear what is the control in Fig. 5e-g.
: Control mouse was injected with the same volume of PBS instead of Serpina1e-V5.
This information is now included in the legend of Figure 5 and Methods in the revised
manuscript.
16) The discussion of scientific background is a bit limited. The authors should better
discuss studies that have examined communication between the skeletal muscle and
the brain.
: We thank the reviewer for helpful comment to improve our manuscript.
Now the revised manuscript includes the summary of previous studies showing functional
roles and related mechanisms of exercise-induced myokines such as FNDC5/irisin and
CTSB in brain functions in the Discussion of the revised manuscript.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript Kim and colleagues identify Serpina1e as a myokine that is released
by muscle into the plasma following 4 weeks of exercise. The also show that delivery
of Serpina1e into the plasma, muscle or hippocampus can replicate the hippocampus-
associated learning and memory enhancement observed following exercise. Overall,
this is a very interesting study. However, several key points should be addressed before
this manuscript would be suitable for publication in Nature Communications.
Major questions:
1. The title of the paper states that Serpina1e “mediates” the exercise-induced
enhancement of hippocampal memory. Likewise, in the abstract they state that
Serpina1e…..”directly” supports long-term memory formation. I disagree that the data
presented here shows this. The authors show that Serpina1e is released by muscle
a muscle after exercise and that Serpina1e
delivery can enhance cognition. However, whether Serpina1e is responsible/required for the exercise-induced
enhancement in cognition has not been shown. To show this direct relationship, one would for example need to knock out
Serpina1e in the muscle and show that exercise can no longer enhance cognition. These statements should all be toned down throughout the manuscript, including the title.
: We thank the reviewer for the valuable comment.
To support our conclusion that Serpina1e mediates exercise-induced enhancement of
hippocampal memory, we tested whether exercise-induced cognitive improvements are
prevented by the reduced Serpina1e expression in skeletal muscles.
To achieve this, we produced a lentivirus containing hCas9 and two gRNAs targeting
Serpina1e (LV-hCas9:T2A:Puro-U6>gRNA-U6>gRNA; S1eKO). This lentivirus was
injected into the limb muscles of wild-type mice, while the lentivirus expressing EGFP and
mCherry (LV-EGFP:T2A:Puro-EF1a>mCherry) was used as a control. Semi-quantitative
RT-PCR analysis of limb muscles injected with the S1eKO lentivirus confirmed that
Serpina1e transcript levels were significantly reduced (Supplementary Fig. 15a-d; Fig.
4h-j in the revised manuscript).
Next, wild-type mice injected with either the S1eKO or control lentivirus were subjected to
novel object recognition (NOR) and contextual fear conditioning (CFC) tests after four
weeks of wheel-running exercise. Our results showed that S1eKO-injected animals without
exercise exhibited normal basal activity and hippocampal memory, indicating that muscle-
derived Serpina1e in non-exercised animals does not affect overall behavioral or cognitive
functions (Fig. 4k, l; Supplementary Fig. 15e-i in the revised manuscript). However,
S1eKO-injected animals failed to show enhanced memory retrieval in NOR and CFC tests,
indicating that exercise-induced cognitive enhancement requires muscle-derived
Serpina1e (Fig. 4k, l in the revised manuscript). Taken together with the results from the
original manuscript, this additional data supports our conclusion that muscle-derived
Serpina1e mediates exercise-induced cognitive enhancement.
2. The authors state that Serpina1e delivery increases neurogenesis in the hippocampal
dentate gyrus. From the data presented in Figure 6 b one is not able to draw this
conclusion. BrdU was injected for the last 5 days of prior to perfusion and BrdU+ cells
quantified. These BrdU+ cells will be a mixture of proliferating neural precursor cells,
immature neurons that may have already become post-mitotic since the first injection
5 days prior, proliferating microglia etc. To be able to quantify adult neurogenesis it
would be best to inject BrdU at the start of the experiment and quantify BrdU+NeuN+
double-positive cells. Alternatively, on the available sections a proliferation marker
such as Ki67 could be used to quantify the proliferating cells (ideally co-labelled with
other markers such as Tbr2 or Sox2) and the immature newborn neurons could be
quantified using DCX staining.
: As the reviewer suggested, we re-assessed the amount of neurogenesis stimulated by
Serpina1e delivery by measuring BrdU/NeuN-double positive cells in the mouse
hippocampus following Serpina1e administration. Our new immunohistochemistry results
showed an increased number of BrdU/NeuN-double positive cells after Serpina1e
administration, while the number of BrdU+/NeuN- cells was unaffected (Fig. 6c-f in the
revised manuscript). These results indicate that Serpina1e-evoked proliferating cells are
neuronally differentiated.
In our experiment, BrdU injection was started 5 days before brain harvest, as done
previously, to examine the effect of chronic Serpina1e administration on neurogenesis. As
the reviewer pointed out, exercise is effective for both the survival and proliferation of
hippocampal neurons (van Praag, 2008, NeuroMolecular Medicine, 10-128-140). Many
studies have shown that chronic exercise (at least three weeks or longer) is most efficient
for the proliferation and survival of hippocampal neurons, as demonstrated by BrdU labeling
at the start of the exercise training. On the other hand, our results, with BrdU injection
starting 5 days prior to the end of Serpina1e administration, reveal only the effect of
Serpina1e on the proliferation of hippocampal cells, not the survival of newborn neurons.
Whether Serpina1e is also effective in upregulating the survival of newborn neurons
remains unclear. Given the crucial role of BDNF signaling in cell survival and the increased
BDNF level after 4 weeks of Serpina1e administration (Fig. 6b in the revised manuscript),
it is possible that Serpina1e administration may also be beneficial for the survival of
newborn neurons.
Additionally, it is unclear if the BrdU counts presented in Fig 6b are per section or per
DG. There is no information in the methods about which sections were stained with
BrdU (i.e., a 1 in 6 series through the whole brain or alike). It is stated that cells were
counted from 12 sections – how were these sections chosen?
: To count the number of BrdU-positive cells, six series of DG slices (at intervals of 120 µm)
from the dorsal hippocampus of each hemisphere (12 sections per mouse) were selected.
The BrdU(+)/NeuN(+) and BrdU(+)/NeuN(-) cell numbers from the six DG slices in each
hemisphere were averaged to produce the mean cell numbers, which are shown as
individual dots in the bar graph (Fig. 6d-f in the revised manuscript).
This detailed information on image analysis has now been included in the Methods section
of the revised manuscript (line 743~747).
The counts state they are # cells/DG and are around 20-30, which if it is BrdU cells per
DG I would expect this count to be hundreds from a young mouse.
: There was our mistake in Fig. 6b in the original manuscript.
The range of Y-axis should be 0-20, and it is now corrected in Fig. 6d in revised
manuscript. This result is consistent with previous reports that the mean number of BrdU-
positive cells in the hippocampus of adult mice is around 15 cells (Zhang et al, 2016, Mol
Med Rep, 14:2231-2237; Kang et al, 2018, Exp Neurobiol, 27(5):419-436).
3. Changes in dendritic arborization could also be assessed in the same mice in the
newborn neurons by performing Sholl analysis on DCX+ cells in vivo. This would
significantly strengthen the in vitro finding which was performed on embryonic cortical
neurons rather than those from the adult hippocampus.
: Instead of DCX staining, we evaluated dendritic arborization in the hippocampal CA1 and
DG areas by measuring Microtubule-associated protein 2 (MAP2)-positive dendrites, as
MAP2 is known to be highly enriched in the dendritic compartment and strongly associated
with branched neurites (Chamak et al., 1987, J Neurosci, 7(10):3163-3170; Chou et al.,
2024, eLife13:RP103127).
To increase the plasma level of Serpina1e, we overexpressed Serpina1e in skeletal
muscles by delivering an AAV virus expressing Serpina1e-EGFP (AAV9-CMV-
mSerpina1e:T2A:EGFP) into the four limbs of WT mice. Control mice were injected with
AAV9-CMV-EGFP. This intramuscular overexpression of Serpina1e was sufficient to
elevate Serpina1e mRNA expression in skeletal muscles and plasma Serpina1e protein
levels (Fig. 4f-g; Supplementary Fig. 14 in the revised manuscript), as well as
hippocampal memory performance (Fig. 4c-e in the revised manuscript). Given our
findings that plasma Serpina1e can be delivered to the hippocampus by crossing the blood-
CSF and blood-brain barriers (Fig. 5a-d; Supplementary Fig. 16 g-i in the revised
manuscript), this intramuscular overexpression of the Serpina1e gene is expected to
upregulate hippocampal Serpina1e protein levels and serve as a useful model for testing
the in vivo effects of Serpina1e on neurite growth.
Z-stack images of MAP2-positive dendrites (775.19 µm x 775.19 µm x 7 µm) were 2D-
projected with maximum intensity to compare the complexity of CA1 dendrites, represented
by MAP2 intensity, between control and muscle Serpina1e-overexpressed mice. Our
results show that the average MAP2 intensity in the hippocampal CA1 and DG area of
muscle Serpina1e-overexpressed mice is significantly higher than that of control mice
(Supplementary Fig. 18 in the revised manuscript). These results indicate that
Serpina1e promotes neuronal dendritic growth in vivo and is consistent with in vitro finding
of elevated neurite growth following treatment with recombinant Serpina1e protein in
cultured neurons.
4. Why were only male mice used in the study? This should be stated in the abstract
and discussed in the discussion.
: To avoid any unexpected effects of sex-dependent physiological and behavioral
phenotypes, we only used male mice in this study.
As human SERPINA1 gene is reported to be a direct target of estrogen receptor and a
predictor of survival rate in patients with breast cancer (Chan et al., 2016, Oncotarget. 6:
25815-25817), it is possible that Serpina1e-induced effects can be influenced by sex-
specific biological mechanisms. Future studies will need to consider comparative
investigations of Serpina1e-mediated cognitive modulation in both sexes.
As the reviewer suggested, we include the statement of the usage of male mice and the
future need of studies addressing the sex-specific role of Serpina1e in cognitive modulation,
in the Abstract (line 27) and Discussion (line 375~376) in the revised manuscript.
Minor points:
1. In the abstract, it is stated that “the beneficial effects of exercise on cognitive
function appear to be mediated by muscle-derived secretory factors”. While muscle is
certainly an important tissue that exerkines are secreted from, there are many others
i.e. hepatokines, adipokines etc.
: Agreeing with the reviewer’s point. We have revised the abstract as following:
line 19: The exercise-induced enhancement of learning and memory is thought to be
regulated not only by improved cardiometabolic and psychosocial health but also
by body‒brain interactions mediated by metabolites and proteins derived from
peripheral organs. Given the prominent role of skeletal muscle during exercise,
muscle-derived factors are believed to mediate the cognitive enhancements induced
by exercise.
2. The sentence “Each dot in the graphs represents a tested mouse” is repeated twice
at the end of each supplemental figure legend.
: We re-examine our manuscript and corrects all errors in the revised manuscript.
3. The discussion section is very brief. There are a lot of discussion points in the results
section that could be moved/expanded on in the discussion.
: We thank the reviewer for valuable feedback to improve our manuscript.
Reflecting all reviewer’s comments, we have expanded the Discussion section by
incorporating the relevant points and limitations of our results as well as future directions
to understand detailed molecular mechanisms underlying Serpina1e-mediated cognitive
enhancements. Please find revised Discussion in the revised manuscript for changes
(marked in red texts).

### Reviewer 1

The authors have thoughtfully responded to the critiques. The revisions have significantly strengthened the manuscript, which will no doubt be an impactful addition to the field.

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript titled "Serpina1e mediates the exercise-induced enhancement of hippocampal memory" presents robust and novel findings identifying Serpina1e as a key myokine mediating the cognitive benefits of exercise. The study is methodologically sound, with comprehensive in vivo and in vitro validation, and the conclusions are well supported by the data.
The work is highly significant for the field, offering insights comparable to previous discoveries such as Irisin, and expanding our understanding of muscle-brain communication. The authors satisfactorily addressed reviewer comments, improving the clarity, methodological transparency, and discussion of their findings. The experimental design, data analysis, and reporting meet the expected standards, with sufficient detail provided to ensure reproducibility. In my evaluation, the manuscript is ready for publication without further revisions.

### Reviewer 3

The authors have made improvements to this interesting manuscript; however, I remain skeptical about several key findings due to significant limitations in both the previous and newly added data.
1) The authors did not conduct the straightforward analysis I requested (previous point 3) to assess whether muscle-contributed Serpina1 is a significant source of the systemic Serpina1 pool, which is primarily expressed in the liver. The authors have access to pan-Serpina1 antibodies and mass spectrometry that could be used for these analyses. At present it remains uncertain whether Serpina 1e secreted by muscle significantly contributes to the circulating pool of Serpina 1e and total Serpina1.
2) The authors now suggest that the muscle pool of Serpina1e plays a key role because they injected lentiviral vectors to knock out Serpina1 in 4 limb muscles, which they claim prevents exercise-induced changes in behavior (discrimination index and freezing). However, these experiments (Fig. 4h-l, as well as others such as those in Fig. 7a-h) are conducted suboptimally, as a control exercise group is not included, leaving it unclear whether the exercise training was performed at optimal levels to induce a response. Additionally, there is no evidence that the lentiviral vectors used are muscle-specific, as they do not appear to carry a muscle-specific promoter and could potentially target Serpina1e in the liver or other tissues. Finally, even if the authors' model is correct and Serpina1e is indeed specifically knocked out in 4 limb muscles, it is still uncertain how this could impair the beneficial effects of exercise on the brain, given that many other muscles, both in the limbs and throughout the body, remain unaffected by the lentiviral vectors (Serpina1e should still increase following exercise in the vast majority of these muscles which are not targeted by the lentiviral vectors and hence promote exercise-induced improvements in behavior).
3) As mentioned in my previous comments, the cognitive assays that are currently utilized in the manuscript (novel object recognition and fear conditioning) are inherently variable. Robust gold-standard assays such as the Morris Water Maze should be performed for at least some of the key experiments.
